segs.p: Yepi te, bhikkhave, ahesuṁ ukkalā vassabhaññā ahetukavādā akiriyavādā natthikavādā, tepime tayo niruttipathe adhivacanapathe paññattipathe na garahitabbaṁ nappaṭikkositabbaṁ amaññiṁsu.
segs.e: Even those who were loud and bold advocates of the doctrines of no-cause, inaction, and nihilism, didn’t imagine that these three scopes of definition should be criticized or rejected.
Why is that?
For fear of being blamed, attacked, provoked, and faulted.”

7. The Perfected Ones
When You Grasp
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṁ desetu yamahaṁ bhagavato dhammaṁ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyyan”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”
“When you grasp, mendicant, you’re bound by Māra.
Not grasping, you’re free from the Wicked One.”
“Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Holy One!”

segs.p: “Yathā kathaṁ pana tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṁ ājānāsī”ti?
segs.e: “But how do you see the detailed meaning of my brief statement?”
“Sir, when you grasp form you’re bound by Māra.
Not grasping, you’re free from the Wicked One.
When you grasp feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness, you’re bound by Māra.
Not grasping, you’re free from the Wicked One.

segs.p: Imassa khvāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavatā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa evaṁ vitthārena atthaṁ ājānāmī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how I understand the detailed meaning of the Buddha’s brief statement.”
“Good, good, mendicant!

segs.p: Sādhu kho tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṁ ājānāsi.
segs.e: It’s good that you understand the detailed meaning of what I’ve said in brief like this.

segs.p: Rūpaṁ kho, bhikkhu, upādiyamāno baddho mārassa;
segs.e: When you grasp form you’re bound by Māra.
Not grasping, you’re free from the Wicked One.
When you grasp feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness, you’re bound by Māra.
Not grasping, you’re free from the Wicked One.

segs.p: Imassa kho, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhittena bhāsitassa evaṁ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti.
segs.e: This is how to see the detailed meaning of what I said in brief.”

segs.p: Atha kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā pakkāmi.
segs.e: And then that mendicant approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

segs.p: Atha kho so bhikkhu eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva—yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṁ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṁ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: Then that mendicant, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

segs.p: “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi.
segs.e: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

segs.p: Aññataro ca pana so bhikkhu arahataṁ ahosīti.
segs.e: And that mendicant became one of the perfected.

“Mendicants, form is impermanent.
What’s impermanent is suffering.

segs.p: yadanattā taṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṁ.

Feeling …

Consciousness is impermanent.
What’s impermanent is suffering.
What’s suffering is not-self.

segs.p: yadanattā taṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṁ.
segs.e: And what’s not-self should be truly seen with right understanding like this: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

segs.p: Evaṁ passaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi … saññāyapi … saṅkhāresupi … viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Nibbindaṁ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṁ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṁ hoti.
segs.e: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

segs.p: Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattāvāsā, yāvatā bhavaggaṁ, ete aggā, ete seṭṭhā lokasmiṁ yadidaṁ arahanto”ti.
segs.e: As far as there are abodes of sentient beings, even up until the pinnacle of existence, the perfected ones are the foremost and the best.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Oh! How happy are the perfected ones!
Craving is not found in them,
the conceit ‘I am’ is cut off,
and the net of delusion is shattered.
They’ve attained imperturbability,
their minds are unclouded,
nothing in the world clings to them,
manifesting divinity, undefiled.
Completely understanding the five aggregates,
their domain is the seven good qualities.
Those true persons are praiseworthy,
the Buddha’s bosom sons.
Endowed with the seven gems,
and trained in the three trainings,
the great heroes live on,
with fear and dread given up.
Endowed with ten factors,
those giants are immersed in samādhi.
They are the best in the world,
craving is not found in them.
The adept’s knowledge has arisen:
‘This bag of bones is my last.’
They are independent of others
in the core of the spiritual path.
They do not waver due to the discriminations,
they’re freed from future lives.
They’ve reached the level of the tamed,
in the world, they’re the winners.
Above, below, all round,
relishing is not found in them.
They roar their lion’s roar:
‘The awakened are supreme in the world!’”

segs.p: “Sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā sāyanhasamayaṁ āsayā nikkhamati; āsayā nikkhamitvā vijambhati; vijambhitvā samantā catuddisā anuviloketi; samantā catuddisā anuviloketvā tikkhattuṁ sīhanādaṁ nadati; tikkhattuṁ sīhanādaṁ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati.
segs.e: “Mendicants, toward evening the lion, king of beasts, emerges from his den, yawns, surveys the four quarters, and roars his lion’s roar three times. Then he sets out on the hunt.

segs.p: Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā pāṇā sīhassa migarañño nadato saddaṁ suṇanti; yebhuyyena bhayaṁ saṁvegaṁ santāsaṁ āpajjanti; bilaṁ bilāsayā pavisanti; dakaṁ dakāsayā pavisanti; vanaṁ vanāsayā pavisanti; ākāsaṁ pakkhino bhajanti.
segs.e: And whatever animals hear the roar of the lion, king of beasts, are typically filled with fear, awe, and terror. They return to their lairs, be they in a hole, the water, or a wood; and the birds take to the air.

segs.p: Yepi te, bhikkhave, rañño nāgā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu, daḷhehi varattehi baddhā, tepi tāni bandhanāni sañchinditvā sampadāletvā bhītā muttakarīsaṁ cajamānā, yena vā tena vā palāyanti.
segs.e: Even the royal elephants, bound with strong harnesses in the villages, towns, and capital cities, break apart their bonds, and urinate and defecate in terror as they flee here and there.

segs.p: Evaṁ mahiddhiko kho, bhikkhave, sīho migarājā tiracchānagatānaṁ pāṇānaṁ, evaṁ mahesakkho, evaṁ mahānubhāvo.
segs.e: That’s how powerful is the lion, king of beasts, over animals, how illustrious and mighty.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yadā tathāgato loke uppajjati arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavā. So dhammaṁ deseti:
segs.e: In the same way, when a Realized One arises in the world—perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed—he teaches the Dhamma:

segs.p: ‘iti rūpaṁ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo;
segs.e: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.
Such is feeling …
Such is perception …
Such are choices …

segs.p: iti viññāṇaṁ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti.
segs.e: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

segs.p: Yepi te, bhikkhave, devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā uccesu vimānesu ciraṭṭhitikā tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṁ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṁ saṁvegaṁ santāsaṁ āpajjanti:
segs.e: Now, there are gods who are long-lived, beautiful, and very happy, lasting long in their divine palaces. When they hear this teaching by the Realized One, they’re typically filled with fear, awe, and terror.

segs.p: ‘aniccāva kira, bho, mayaṁ samānā niccamhāti amaññimha.
segs.e: ‘Oh no! It turns out we’re impermanent, though we thought we were permanent!

segs.p: Addhuvāva kira, bho, mayaṁ samānā dhuvamhāti amaññimha.
segs.e: It turns out we don’t last, though we thought we were everlasting!

segs.p: Asassatāva kira, bho, mayaṁ samānā sassatamhāti amaññimha.
segs.e: It turns out we’re transient, though we thought we were eternal!

segs.p: Mayampi kira, bho, aniccā addhuvā asassatā sakkāyapariyāpannā’ti.
segs.e: It turns out that we’re impermanent, not lasting, transient, and included within substantial reality.’

segs.p: Evaṁ mahiddhiko kho, bhikkhave, tathāgato sadevakassa lokassa, evaṁ mahesakkho, evaṁ mahānubhāvo”ti.
segs.e: That’s how powerful is the Realized One in the world with its gods, how illustrious and mighty.”
That is what the Buddha said.
Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“The Buddha, the unrivaled Teacher
in all the world with its gods,
rolls forth the Wheel of Dhamma
from his own insight:
substantial reality, its cessation,
the origin of substantial reality,
and the noble eightfold path
that leads to the stilling of suffering.
And then the long-lived gods,
so beautiful and glorious,
are afraid and full of terror,
like the other beasts when they hear a lion.
‘We haven’t passed beyond substantial reality!
It turns out we’re impermanent!’
So they say when they hear the word
of the perfected one, free and unaffected.”
Linked Discourses 22.79
8. Bitable
Bitable
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā anekavihitaṁ pubbenivāsaṁ anussaramānā anussaranti sabbete pañcupādānakkhandhe anussaranti etesaṁ vā aññataraṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, whatever ascetics and brahmins recollect many kinds of past lives, all recollect the five grasping aggregates, or one of them.
What five?
‘I had such form in the past.’

segs.p: iti vā hi, bhikkhave, anussaramāno rūpaṁyeva anussarati.
segs.e: Recollecting thus, it’s only form that they recollect.
‘I had such feeling …

segs.p: iti vā hi, bhikkhave, anussaramāno vedanaṁyeva anussarati.

segs.e: perception …
choices …
consciousness in the past.’

segs.p: iti vā hi, bhikkhave, anussaramāno viññāṇameva anussarati.
segs.e: Recollecting thus, it’s only consciousness that they recollect.
And why do you call it form?
It’s deformed; that’s why it’s called ‘form’.
Deformed by what?

segs.p: Sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jighacchāyapi ruppati, pipāsāyapi ruppati, ḍaṁsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassenapi ruppati.
segs.e: Deformed by cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and deformed by the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles.
It’s deformed; that’s why it’s called ‘form’.
And why do you call it feeling?
It feels; that’s why it’s called ‘feeling’.
And what does it feel?

segs.p: Sukhampi vedayati, dukkhampi vedayati, adukkhamasukhampi vedayati.
segs.e: It feels pleasure, pain, and neutral.
It feels; that’s why it’s called ‘feeling’.
And why do you call it perception?
It perceives; that’s why it’s called ‘perception’.
And what does it perceive?

segs.p: Nīlampi sañjānāti, pītakampi sañjānāti, lohitakampi sañjānāti, odātampi sañjānāti.
segs.e: It perceives blue, yellow, red, and white.
It perceives; that’s why it’s called ‘perception’.
And why do you call them choices?
Choices produce conditioned phenomena; that’s why they’re called ‘choices’.
And what are the conditioned phenomena that they produce?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ rūpattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, vedanaṁ vedanattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, saññaṁ saññattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, saṅkhāre saṅkhārattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti, viññāṇaṁ viññāṇattāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharonti.
segs.e: Form is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into form. Feeling is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into feeling. Perception is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into perception. Choices are conditioned phenomena; choices are what make them into choices. Consciousness is a conditioned phenomenon; choices are what make it into consciousness.
Choices produce conditioned phenomena; that’s why they’re called ‘choices’.
And why do you call it consciousness?
It cognizes; that’s why it’s called ‘consciousness’.
And what does it cognize?

segs.p: Ambilampi vijānāti, tittakampi vijānāti, kaṭukampi vijānāti, madhurampi vijānāti, khārikampi vijānāti, akhārikampi vijānāti, loṇikampi vijānāti, aloṇikampi vijānāti.
segs.e: It cognizes sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, hot, mild, salty, and bland.
It cognizes; that’s why it’s called ‘consciousness’.

segs.p: Tatra, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: A learned noble disciple reflects on this:
‘Currently I’m bitten by form.

segs.p: Atītampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva rūpena khajjiṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannena rūpena khajjāmi.
segs.e: In the past I was also bitten by form just like now.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana anāgataṁ rūpaṁ abhinandeyyaṁ, anāgatampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva rūpena khajjeyyaṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannena rūpena khajjāmī’ti.
segs.e: If I were to look forward to enjoying form in the future, I’d be bitten by form in the future just as I am today.’

segs.p: So iti paṭisaṅkhāya atītasmiṁ rūpasmiṁ anapekkho hoti;
segs.e: Reflecting like this they are not concerned with past form,
they don’t look forward to enjoying future form,

segs.p: paccuppannassa rūpassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
segs.e: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.
‘Currently I’m bitten by feeling …

segs.p: Atītampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva vedanāya khajjiṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannāya vedanāya khajjāmi.
Ahañceva kho pana anāgataṁ vedanaṁ abhinandeyyaṁ;
anāgatampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva vedanāya khajjeyyaṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannāya vedanāya khajjāmī’ti.
So iti paṭisaṅkhāya atītāya vedanāya anapekkho hoti;
paccuppannāya vedanāya nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

segs.e: perception …
choices …

segs.p: Atītampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva saṅkhārehi khajjiṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannehi saṅkhārehi khajjāmīti.
Ahañceva kho pana anāgate saṅkhāre abhinandeyyaṁ;
anāgatampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva saṅkhārehi khajjeyyaṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannehi saṅkhārehi khajjāmī’ti.
So iti paṭisaṅkhāya atītesu saṅkhāresu anapekkho hoti;
paccuppannānaṁ saṅkhārānaṁ nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.

segs.e: consciousness.

segs.p: Atītampi addhānaṁ evameva viññāṇena khajjiṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannena viññāṇena khajjāmi.
segs.e: In the past I was also bitten by consciousness just like now.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana anāgataṁ viññāṇaṁ abhinandeyyaṁ;
segs.e: If I were to look forward to enjoying consciousness in the future, I’d be bitten by consciousness in the future just as I am today.’

segs.p: anāgatampāhaṁ addhānaṁ evameva viññāṇena khajjeyyaṁ, seyyathāpi etarahi paccuppannena viññāṇena khajjāmī’ti.
So iti paṭisaṅkhāya atītasmiṁ viññāṇasmiṁ anapekkho hoti;
segs.e: Reflecting like this they are not concerned with past consciousness,
they don’t look forward to enjoying future consciousness,

segs.p: paccuppannassa viññāṇassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti.
segs.e: and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
What do you think, mendicants?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”

segs.p: “Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, yaṁ kiñci rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ rūpaṁ: ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṁ.
segs.e: “So you should truly see any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
You should truly see any kind of feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ …pe… yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ viññāṇaṁ: ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṁ.
segs.e: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako apacināti, no ācināti;
segs.e: This is called a noble disciple who gets rid of and doesn’t accumulate;
who gives up and doesn’t grasp;
who unmeshes and doesn’t enmesh;
who dissipates and doesn’t get clouded.
And what things do they get rid of and not accumulate?
They get rid of form and don’t accumulate it.
They get rid of feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness and don’t accumulate it.
And what things do they give up and not grasp?
They give up form and don’t grasp it.
They give up feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness and don’t grasp it.
And what things do they unmesh and not enmesh?
They unmesh form and don’t enmesh it.
They unmesh feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness and don’t enmesh it.
And what things do they dissipate and not get clouded by?
They dissipate form and don’t get clouded by it.
They dissipate feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness and don’t get clouded by it.

segs.p: Evaṁ passaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi … saññāyapi … saṅkhāresupi … viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Nibbindaṁ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṁ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṁ hoti.
segs.e: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.

segs.p: ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this place.’

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nevācināti na apacināti, apacinitvā ṭhito; neva pajahati na upādiyati, pajahitvā ṭhito; neva visineti na ussineti, visinetvā ṭhito; neva vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti vidhūpetvā ṭhito
segs.e: This is called a mendicant who neither gets rid of nor accumulates, but remains after getting rid. They neither give up nor grasp, but remain after giving up. They neither unmesh nor enmesh, but remain after unmeshing. They neither dissipate nor get clouded, but remain after dissipating.

segs.p: Kiñca nevācināti na apacināti, apacinitvā ṭhito?
segs.e: And what things do they neither get rid of nor accumulate, but remain after getting rid of them?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ nevācināti na apacināti, apacinitvā ṭhito;
segs.e: They neither get rid of nor accumulate form, but remain after getting rid of it.
They neither get rid of nor accumulate feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ nevācināti na apacināti, apacinitvā ṭhito.
segs.e: consciousness, but remain after getting rid of it.

segs.p: Kiñca neva pajahati na upādiyati, pajahitvā ṭhito?
segs.e: And what things do they neither give up nor grasp, but remain after giving them up?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ neva pajahati na upādiyati, pajahitvā ṭhito;
segs.e: They neither give up nor grasp form, but remain after giving it up.
They neither give up nor grasp feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ neva pajahati na upādiyati, pajahitvā ṭhito.
segs.e: consciousness, but remain after giving it up.

segs.p: Kiñca neva visineti na ussineti, visinetvā ṭhito?
segs.e: And what things do they neither discard nor amass, but remain after discarding them?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ neva visineti na ussineti, visinetvā ṭhito;
segs.e: They neither unmesh nor enmesh form, but remain after unmeshing it.
They neither unmesh nor enmesh feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ neva visineti na ussineti, visinetvā ṭhito.
segs.e: consciousness, but remain after unmeshing it.

segs.p: Kiñca neva vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti, vidhūpetvā ṭhito?
segs.e: And what things do they neither dissipate nor get clouded by, but remain after dissipating them?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ neva vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti, vidhūpetvā ṭhito;
segs.e: They neither dissipate nor get clouded by form, but remain after dissipating it.
They neither dissipate nor get clouded by feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ neva vidhūpeti na sandhūpeti, vidhūpetvā ṭhito.
segs.e: consciousness, but remain after dissipating it.

segs.p: Evaṁvimuttacittaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṁ saindā devā sabrahmakā sapajāpatikā ārakāva namassanti:
segs.e: When a mendicant’s mind is freed like this, the gods together with Indra, the Divinity, and the Progenitor worship them from afar:
‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred!
Homage to you, supreme among men!
We don’t understand
the basis of your absorption.’”
Linked Discourses 22.80
8. Bitable
Beggars

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṁ nigrodhārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā kismiñcideva pakaraṇe bhikkhusaṅghaṁ paṇāmetvā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kapilavatthuṁ piṇḍāya pāvisi.
segs.e: Then the Buddha, having dismissed the mendicant Saṅgha for some reason, robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms.

segs.p: Kapilavatthusmiṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena mahāvanaṁ tenupasaṅkami divāvihārāya.
segs.e: He wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu. After the meal, on his return from almsround, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s meditation,

segs.p: Mahāvanaṁ ajjhogāhetvā beluvalaṭṭhikāya mūle divāvihāraṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: plunged deep into it, and sat at the root of a young wood-apple tree to meditate.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,
“I have purged the mendicant Saṅgha.

segs.p: Santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṁ dhammavinayaṁ.
segs.e: But there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training.

segs.p: Tesaṁ mamaṁ apassantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.
segs.e: Not seeing me they may change and fall apart.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi nāma vacchassa taruṇassa mātaraṁ apassantassa siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo;
segs.e: If a young calf doesn’t see its mother it may change and fall apart. …

segs.p: evameva santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṁ dhammavinayaṁ tesaṁ mamaṁ apassantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.
Seyyathāpi nāma bījānaṁ taruṇānaṁ udakaṁ alabhantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo;
segs.e: Or if young seedlings don’t get water they may change and fall apart.
In the same way, there are mendicants here who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training.

segs.p: tesaṁ mamaṁ alabhantānaṁ dassanāya siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.
segs.e: Not seeing me they may change and fall apart.

segs.p: Yannūnāhaṁ yatheva mayā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho anuggahito, evameva etarahi anuggaṇheyyaṁ bhikkhusaṅghan”ti.
segs.e: Why don’t I support the mendicant Saṅgha now as I did in the past?”

segs.p: Atha kho brahmā sahampati bhagavato cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṁ vā bāhaṁ pasāreyya pasāritaṁ vā bāhaṁ samiñjeyya; evameva—brahmaloke antarahito bhagavato purato pāturahosi.
segs.e: Then the divinity Sahampati knew the Buddha’s train of thought. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha.

segs.p: Atha kho brahmā sahampati ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!
The Buddha has purged the mendicant Saṅgha.

segs.p: Santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṁ dhammavinayaṁ.
segs.e: But there are mendicants who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training. …

segs.p: Tesaṁ bhagavantaṁ apassantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.
Seyyathāpi nāma vacchassa taruṇassa mātaraṁ apassantassa siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo;
evameva santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṁ dhammavinayaṁ tesaṁ bhagavantaṁ apassantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.
Seyyathāpi nāma bījānaṁ taruṇānaṁ udakaṁ alabhantānaṁ siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo;
evameva santettha bhikkhū navā acirapabbajitā adhunāgatā imaṁ dhammavinayaṁ, tesaṁ bhagavantaṁ alabhantānaṁ dassanāya siyā aññathattaṁ siyā vipariṇāmo.

segs.e: May the Buddha be happy with the mendicant Saṅgha!
May the Buddha welcome the mendicant Saṅgha!

segs.p: Yatheva bhagavatā pubbe bhikkhusaṅgho anuggahito, evameva etarahi anuggaṇhātu bhikkhusaṅghan”ti.
segs.e: May the Buddha support the mendicant Saṅgha now as he did in the past!”
The Buddha consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho brahmā sahampati bhagavato adhivāsanaṁ viditvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā tatthevantaradhāyi.
segs.e: Then the divinity Sahampati, knowing that the Buddha had consented, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena nigrodhārāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the Banyan Tree Monastery, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Nisajja kho bhagavā tathārūpaṁ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṁ abhisaṅkhāsi yathā te bhikkhū ekadvīhikāya sārajjamānarūpā yenāhaṁ tenupasaṅkameyyuṁ.
segs.e: Then he used his psychic power to will that the mendicants would come to him timidly, alone or in pairs.

segs.p: Tepi bhikkhū ekadvīhikāya sārajjamānarūpā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinne kho te bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Those mendicants approached the Buddha timidly, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:
“This is the last of lifestyles, mendicants, namely relying on alms.

segs.p: Abhisāpoyaṁ, bhikkhave, lokasmiṁ piṇḍolo vicarasi pattapāṇīti.
segs.e: The world curses you: ‘You beggar, walking bowl in hand!’

segs.p: Tañca kho etaṁ, bhikkhave, kulaputtā upenti atthavasikā, atthavasaṁ paṭicca;
segs.e: Yet earnest gentlemen take it up for a good reason.

segs.p: neva rājābhinītā, na corābhinītā, na iṇaṭṭā, na bhayaṭṭā, na ājīvikāpakatā;
segs.e: Not to escape a summons by a king or a summons for a bandit, or because you were in debt or in fear, or in order to make a living.

segs.p: api ca kho otiṇṇāmha jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi dukkhotiṇṇā dukkhaparetā
segs.e: But because they’re swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They’re swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

segs.p: appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethāti.
segs.e: And they think, ‘Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’
That’s how this gentleman has gone forth.

segs.p: So ca hoti abhijjhālu kāmesu tibbasārāgo byāpannacitto paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo muṭṭhassati asampajāno asamāhito vibbhantacitto pākatindriyo.
segs.e: Yet they covet sensual pleasures; they’re infatuated, full of ill will and malicious intent. They are unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying mind and undisciplined faculties.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, chavālātaṁ ubhatopadittaṁ majjhe gūthagataṁ, neva gāme kaṭṭhatthaṁ pharati, nāraññe kaṭṭhatthaṁ pharati.
segs.e: Suppose there was a firebrand for lighting a funeral pyre, burning at both ends, and smeared with dung in the middle. It couldn’t be used as timber either in the village or the wilderness.

segs.p: Tathūpamāhaṁ, bhikkhave, imaṁ puggalaṁ vadāmi gihibhogā ca parihīno, sāmaññatthañca na paripūreti.
segs.e: I say that individual is just like this. They’ve missed out on the pleasures of the lay life, and haven’t fulfilled the goal of the ascetic life.
There are these three unskillful thoughts.
Sensual, malicious, and cruel thoughts.

segs.p: Ime ca bhikkhave, tayo akusalavitakkā kva aparisesā nirujjhanti?
segs.e: And where do these three unskillful thoughts cease without remainder?

segs.p: Catūsu vā satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittassa viharato animittaṁ vā samādhiṁ bhāvayato.
segs.e: In those who meditate with their mind firmly established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation; or who develop signless immersion.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva animitto samādhi bhāvetuṁ.
segs.e: This is quite enough motivation to develop signless immersion.

segs.p: Animitto, bhikkhave, samādhi bhāvito bahulīkato mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṁso.
segs.e: When signless immersion is developed and cultivated it is very fruitful and beneficial.
There are these two views.
Views favoring existence and views favoring nonexistence.

segs.p: Tatra kho, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: A learned noble disciple reflects on this:

segs.p: ‘atthi nu kho taṁ kiñci lokasmiṁ yamahaṁ upādiyamāno na vajjavā assan’ti?
segs.e: ‘Is there anything in the world that I could grasp without fault?’
They understand:

segs.p: ‘natthi nu kho taṁ kiñci lokasmiṁ yamahaṁ upādiyamāno na vajjavā assaṁ.
segs.e: ‘There’s nothing in the world that I could grasp without fault.
For in grasping I would grasp only at form, feeling,
perception,
choices, or consciousness.
That grasping of mine would be a condition for continued existence.
Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth.
Rebirth is a requirement for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be.
That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’
What do you think, mendicants?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?” …
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”
Linked Discourses 22.81
8. Bitable
At Pārileyyaka

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kosambiyaṁ viharati ghositārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kosambiṁ piṇḍāya pāvisi.
segs.e: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms.

segs.p: Kosambiyaṁ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṁ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sāmaṁ senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṁ eko adutiyo cārikaṁ pakkāmi.
segs.e: After the meal, on his return from almsround, he set his lodgings in order himself. Taking his bowl and robe, without informing his supporters or taking leave of the mendicant Saṅgha, he set out to go wandering alone, with no companion.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu acirapakkantassa bhagavato yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then, not long after the Buddha had left, one of the mendicants went to Venerable Ānanda and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “esāvuso ānanda, bhagavā sāmaṁ senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṁ eko adutiyo cārikaṁ pakkanto”ti.

“Yasmiṁ, āvuso, samaye bhagavā sāmaṁ senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṁ eko adutiyo cārikaṁ pakkamati, ekova bhagavā tasmiṁ samaye viharitukāmo hoti;
segs.e: Ānanda said, “Reverend, when the Buddha leaves like this it means he wants to stay alone.

segs.p: na bhagavā tasmiṁ samaye kenaci anubandhitabbo hotī”ti.
segs.e: At this time no one should follow him.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā anupubbena cārikaṁ caramāno yena pālileyyakaṁ tadavasari.
segs.e: Then the Buddha, traveling stage by stage, arrived at Pārileyyaka,

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ bhagavā pālileyyake viharati bhaddasālamūle.
segs.e: where he stayed at the root of a sacred sal tree.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṁ sammodiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him,

segs.p: “cirassutā kho no, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammī kathā;
segs.e: “Reverend, it’s been a long time since we’ve heard a Dhamma talk from the Buddha.

segs.p: icchāma mayaṁ, āvuso ānanda, bhagavato sammukhā dhammiṁ kathaṁ sotun”ti.
segs.e: We wish to hear a Dhamma talk from the Buddha.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ yena pālileyyakaṁ bhaddasālamūlaṁ yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then Venerable Ānanda together with those mendicants went to Pārileyyaka to see the Buddha. They bowed and sat down to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinne kho te bhikkhū bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṁsesi.
segs.e: and the Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired them with a Dhamma talk.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Now at that time one of the monks had the thought,

segs.p: “kathaṁ nu kho jānato kathaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hotī”ti?
segs.e: “How do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the mendicants:
“Mendicants, I’ve taught the Dhamma analytically.
I’ve analytically taught the four kinds of mindfulness meditation,
the four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties,
the five powers,
the seven awakening factors,
and the noble eightfold path.

segs.p: Evaṁ vicayaso desito, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo.
segs.e: That’s how I’ve taught the Dhamma analytically.

segs.p: Evaṁ vicayaso desite kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme atha ca panidhekaccassa bhikkhuno evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Though I’ve taught the Dhamma analytically, still a certain mendicant present here has this thought:

segs.p: ‘kathaṁ nu kho jānato kathaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hotī’ti?
segs.e: ‘How do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?’

segs.p: Kathañca, bhikkhave, jānato kathaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti?
segs.e: And how, mendicants, do you know and see in order to end the defilements without delay?

segs.p: Idha bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṁ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṁ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto
segs.e: Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.
They regard form as self.

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon.

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
segs.e: And what’s the source, origin, birthplace, and inception of that conditioned phenomenon?

segs.p: Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
segs.e: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.
That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

segs.p: Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
And that craving,

segs.p: Sāpi vedanā, sopi phasso anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: that feeling, that contact,
and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

segs.p: Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
segs.e: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

segs.p: Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati;
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self,

segs.p: api ca kho rūpavantaṁ attānaṁ samanupassati.
segs.e: but they still regard self as possessing form.

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṁ attānaṁ samanupassati;
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form,

segs.p: api ca kho attani rūpaṁ samanupassati.
segs.e: but they still regard form in self.

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṁ attānaṁ samanupassati, na attani rūpaṁ samanupassati;
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self,

segs.p: api ca kho rūpasmiṁ attānaṁ samanupassati.
segs.e: but they still regard self in form.

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon. …

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
Evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato …pe… āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṁ attānaṁ, na attani rūpaṁ, na rūpasmiṁ attānaṁ samanupassati;
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form.

segs.p: api ca kho vedanaṁ attato samanupassati, api ca kho vedanāvantaṁ attānaṁ samanupassati, api ca kho attani vedanaṁ samanupassati, api ca kho vedanāya attānaṁ samanupassati;
segs.e: But they regard feeling as self …
perception as self …

segs.p: api ca kho saṅkhāre attato samanupassati, api ca kho saṅkhāravantaṁ attānaṁ samanupassati, api ca kho attani saṅkhāre samanupassati, api ca kho saṅkhāresu attānaṁ samanupassati;
segs.e: choices as self …

segs.p: api ca kho viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, api ca kho viññāṇavantaṁ attānaṁ, api ca kho attani viññāṇaṁ, api ca kho viññāṇasmiṁ attānaṁ samanupassati.
segs.e: consciousness as self …

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that regarding is just a conditioned phenomenon.
And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon?

segs.p: Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
segs.e: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.
That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

segs.p: Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
And that craving,
that feeling,
that contact,
and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
segs.e: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

segs.p: Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati,
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form
or feeling
or perception
or choices
or consciousness as self.
Still, they have such a view:

segs.p: ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti.
segs.e: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, sassatadiṭṭhi saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that eternalist view is just a conditioned phenomenon.
And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon? …

segs.p: evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
segs.e: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

segs.p: Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati,
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form
or feeling
or perception
or choices
or consciousness as self.
Nor do they have such a view:

segs.p: ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti.
segs.e: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’
Still, they have such a view:

segs.p: ‘no cassaṁ no ca me siyā nābhavissaṁ na me bhavissatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘I might not be, and it might not be mine. I will not be, and it will not be mine.’

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, ucchedadiṭṭhi saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: But that annihilationist view is just a conditioned phenomenon.

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
segs.e: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon? …

segs.p: Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco …pe…
evampi kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hoti.
segs.e: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.

segs.p: Na heva kho rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na vedanaṁ …
segs.e: Perhaps they don’t regard form or feeling
or perception
or choices
or consciousness as self.

segs.p: na viññāṇasmiṁ attato samanupassati, nāpi evaṁdiṭṭhi hoti:
segs.e: Nor do they have such a view:

segs.p: ‘so attā so loko, so pecca bhavissāmi nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo’ti;
segs.e: ‘The self and the cosmos are one and the same. After death I will be that, permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.’
Nor do they have such a view:

segs.p: ‘no cassaṁ no ca me siyā nābhavissaṁ na me bhavissatī’ti;
segs.e: ‘I might not be, and it might not be mine. I will not be, and it will not be mine.’

segs.p: api ca kho kaṅkhī hoti vicikicchī aniṭṭhaṅgato saddhamme.
segs.e: Still, they have doubts and uncertainties. They’re undecided about the true teaching.

segs.p: Yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, kaṅkhitā vicikicchitā aniṭṭhaṅgatatā saddhamme saṅkhāro so.
segs.e: That doubt and uncertainty, the indecision about the true teaching, is just a conditioned phenomenon.

segs.p: So pana saṅkhāro kiṁnidāno kiṁsamudayo kiṁjātiko kiṁpabhavo?
segs.e: And what’s the source of that conditioned phenomenon?

segs.p: Avijjāsamphassajena, bhikkhave, vedayitena phuṭṭhassa assutavato puthujjanassa uppannā taṇhā;
segs.e: When an unlearned ordinary person is struck by feelings born of contact with ignorance, craving arises.
That conditioned phenomenon is born from that.

segs.p: Iti kho, bhikkhave, sopi saṅkhāro anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: So that conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
And that craving,
that feeling,
that contact,
and that ignorance are also impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṁ passato anantarā āsavānaṁ khayo hotī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how you should know and see in order to end the defilements without delay.”
Linked Discourses 22.82
8. Bitable
A Full Moon Night

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra’s mother in the Eastern Monastery, together with a large Saṅgha of monks.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā tadahuposathe pannarase puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ajjhokāse nisinno hoti.
segs.e: Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṁsaṁ uttarāsaṅgaṁ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṁ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then one of the monks rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said:

segs.p: “puccheyyāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavantaṁ kiñcideva desaṁ, sace me bhagavā okāsaṁ karoti pañhassa veyyākaraṇāyā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, I’d like to ask the Buddha about a certain point, if you’d take the time to answer.”

segs.p: “Tena hi tvaṁ, bhikkhu, sake āsane nisīditvā puccha yadākaṅkhasī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, monk, take your own seat and ask what you wish.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā sake āsane nisīditvā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” replied that monk. He took his seat and said to the Buddha:
“Sir, are these the five grasping aggregates, that is:
form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness?”
“Yes, they are,” replied the Buddha.

segs.p: “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṁ uttariṁ pañhaṁ apucchi:
segs.e: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:
“But sir, what is the root of these five grasping aggregates?”
“These five grasping aggregates are rooted in desire.” …

segs.p: taññeva nu kho, bhante, upādānaṁ te pañcupādānakkhandhā udāhu aññatra pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi upādānan”ti?
segs.e: “But sir, is that grasping the exact same thing as the five grasping aggregates? Or is grasping one thing and the five grasping aggregates another?”

segs.p: “Na kho, bhikkhu, taññeva upādānaṁ te pañcupādānakkhandhā nāpi aññatra pañcahi upādānakkhandhehi upādānaṁ, api ca yo tattha chandarāgo taṁ tattha upādānan”ti.
segs.e: “Neither. Rather, the desire and greed for them is the grasping there.”

segs.p: “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu …pe… uttariṁ pañhaṁ apucchi:
segs.e: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:
“But sir, can there be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates?”
“There can,” said the Buddha.
“It’s when someone thinks:

segs.p: ‘evaṁrūpo siyaṁ anāgatamaddhānaṁ, evaṁvedano siyaṁ anāgatamaddhānaṁ, evaṁsañño siyaṁ anāgatamaddhānaṁ, evaṁsaṅkhāro siyaṁ anāgatamaddhānaṁ, evaṁviññāṇo siyaṁ anāgatamaddhānan’ti.
segs.e: ‘In the future, may I be of such form, such feeling, such perception, such choices, and such consciousness!’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhu, siyā pañcupādānakkhandhesu chandarāgavemattatā”ti.
segs.e: That’s how there can be disparity in desire and greed for the five grasping aggregates.”

segs.p: “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu …pe… uttariṁ pañhaṁ apucchi:
segs.e: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:
“Sir, what is the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates?”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kiñci, bhikkhu, rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, ayaṁ vuccati rūpakkhandho.
segs.e: “Any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of form.
Any kind of feeling at all …
Any kind of perception at all …
Any kind of choices at all …

segs.p: yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, ayaṁ vuccati viññāṇakkhandho.
segs.e: Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
That’s the scope of the term ‘aggregates’ as applied to the aggregates.”
Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:

segs.p: “Ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāya;
segs.e: “What is the cause, sir, what is the reason why the aggregate of form is found?

segs.p: ko hetu ko paccayo vedanākkhandhassa paññāpanāya;
segs.e: What is the cause, what is the reason why the aggregate of feeling …

segs.p: ko hetu ko paccayo saññākkhandhassa paññāpanāya;
segs.e: perception …

segs.p: ko hetu ko paccayo saṅkhārakkhandhassa paññāpanāya;
segs.e: choices …

segs.p: ko hetu ko paccayo viññāṇakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”ti?
segs.e: consciousness is found?”

segs.p: “Cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetu, cattāro mahābhūtā paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāya.
segs.e: “The four principal states are the reason why the aggregate of form is found.

segs.p: Phasso hetu phasso paccayo vedanākkhandhassa paññāpanāya.
segs.e: Contact is the reason why the aggregates of feeling,

segs.p: Phasso hetu phasso paccayo saññākkhandhassa paññāpanāya.
segs.e: perception,

segs.p: Phasso hetu, phasso paccayo saṅkhārakkhandhassa paññāpanāya.
segs.e: and choices are found.

segs.p: Nāmarūpaṁ hetu, nāmarūpaṁ paccayo viññāṇakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”ti.
segs.e: Name and form are the reasons why the aggregate of consciousness is found.”
Saying “Good, sir”, that monk asked another question:
“Sir, how does substantialist view come about?”

segs.p: “Idha, bhikkhu, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṁ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṁ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto
segs.e: “It’s when an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

segs.p: rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā rūpaṁ, rūpasmiṁ vā attānaṁ;
segs.e: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
They regard feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā viññāṇaṁ, viññāṇasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
That’s how substantialist view comes about.”
Saying “Good, sir”, that monk … asked another question:
“But sir, how does substantialist view not come about?”

segs.p: “Idha, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako ariyānaṁ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṁ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto
segs.e: “It’s when a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

segs.p: na rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; na attani vā rūpaṁ, na rūpasmiṁ vā attānaṁ;
segs.e: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
They don’t regard feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: na viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; na attani vā viññāṇaṁ, na viññāṇasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhu, sakkāyadiṭṭhi na hotī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how substantialist view does not come about.”
Saying “Good, sir”, that monk … asked another question:

segs.p: “Ko nu kho, bhante, rūpassa assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇaṁ;
segs.e: “Sir, what’s the gratification, the drawback, and the escape when it comes to form,
feeling,
perception,
choices,

segs.p: ko viññāṇassa assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: and consciousness?”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kho, bhikkhu, rūpaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ—ayaṁ rūpassa assādo.
segs.e: “The pleasure and happiness that arise from form: this is its gratification.

segs.p: Yaṁ rūpaṁ aniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ—ayaṁ rūpassa ādīnavo.
segs.e: That form is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

segs.p: Yo rūpasmiṁ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ—idaṁ rūpassa nissaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for form: this is its escape.
The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: yaṁ viññāṇaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ—ayaṁ viññāṇassa assādo.
segs.e: consciousness: this is its gratification.

segs.p: Yaṁ viññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ—ayaṁ viññāṇassa ādīnavo.
segs.e: That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

segs.p: Yo viññāṇasmiṁ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ—idaṁ viññāṇassa nissaraṇan”ti.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for consciousness: this is its escape.”

segs.p: “Sādhu, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinanditvā anumoditvā bhagavantaṁ uttariṁ pañhaṁ apucchi:
segs.e: Saying “Good, sir”, that monk approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. Then he asked another question:

segs.p: “Kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kiñci, bhikkhu, rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ rūpaṁ: ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: “One truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
One truly sees any kind of feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ viññāṇaṁ: ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
segs.e: Now at that time one of the monks had the thought:

segs.p: “iti kira bho rūpaṁ anattā, vedanā … saññā … saṅkhārā … viññāṇaṁ anattā;
segs.e: “So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.
Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassa bhikkhuno cetasā ceto parivitakkamaññāya bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha, knowing that monk’s train of thought, addressed the monks:

segs.p: “Ṭhānaṁ kho panetaṁ, bhikkhave, vijjati yaṁ idhekacco moghapuriso avidvā avijjāgato taṇhādhipateyyena cetasā satthusāsanaṁ atidhāvitabbaṁ maññeyya.
segs.e: “It’s possible that some futile person here—unknowing and ignorant, his mind dominated by craving—thinks he can overstep the Teacher’s instructions. He thinks:

segs.p: ‘Iti kira, bho, rūpaṁ anattā, vedanā … saññā … saṅkhārā … viññāṇaṁ anattā.
segs.e: ‘So it seems, worthy sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self.
Then how will the deeds done by not-self affect the self?’

segs.p: Paṭipucchāvinītā kho me tumhe, bhikkhave, tatra tatra tesu tesu dhammesu.
segs.e: Now, monks, you have been educated by me in questioning with regard to all these things in all such cases.
What do you think, monks?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”
“Two on the aggregates; exactly the same; <j>and can there be;
on the term; and on the cause;
two questions on substantial reality;
gratification; and that with consciousness:
these are the ten questions
the monk came to ask.”
Linked Discourses 22.83
9. Senior Mendicants
With Ānanda
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tatra kho āyasmā ānando bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: There Ānanda addressed the mendicants:
“Reverends, mendicants!”

segs.p: “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato ānandassa paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Reverend,” they replied.
Ānanda said this:

segs.p: “Puṇṇo nāma, āvuso, āyasmā mantāṇiputto amhākaṁ navakānaṁ sataṁ bahūpakāro hoti.
segs.e: “Reverends, the venerable named Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī was very helpful to me when I was just ordained.
He gave me this advice:

segs.p: ‘upādāya, āvuso ānanda, asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.
segs.e: ‘Reverend Ānanda, the thought “I am” occurs because of grasping, not without grasping.

segs.p: Kiñca upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya?
segs.e: Grasping what?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.
segs.e: The thought “I am” occurs because of grasping form,
feeling,
perception,
choices,

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.
segs.e: and consciousness, not without grasping.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso ānanda, itthī vā puriso vā daharo yuvā maṇḍanakajātiko ādāse vā parisuddhe pariyodāte acche vā udakapatte sakaṁ mukhanimittaṁ paccavekkhamāno upādāya passeyya, no anupādāya;
segs.e: Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and they check their own reflection in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. They’d look because of grasping, not without grasping.

segs.p: evameva kho, āvuso ānanda, rūpaṁ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.
segs.e: In the same way, the thought “I am” occurs because of grasping form,
feeling,
perception,
choices,

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ upādāya asmīti hoti, no anupādāya.
segs.e: and consciousness, not without grasping.
What do you think, Reverend Ānanda?
Is form permanent or impermanent?’
‘Impermanent, reverend.’
‘Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?’
‘Impermanent, reverend.’ …
‘So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: “… there is nothing further for this place.”’

segs.p: Puṇṇo nāma, āvuso, āyasmā mantāṇiputto amhākaṁ navakānaṁ sataṁ bahūpakāro hoti.
segs.e: Reverends, the venerable named Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī was very helpful to me when I was just ordained.
He gave me this advice.

segs.p: Idañca pana me āyasmato puṇṇassa mantāṇiputtassa dhammadesanaṁ sutvā dhammo abhisamito”ti.
segs.e: And when I heard this teaching from Venerable Puṇṇa son of Mantāṇī, I comprehended the teaching.”
Linked Discourses 22.84
9. Senior Mendicants
With Tissa
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā tisso bhagavato pitucchāputto sambahulānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ evamāroceti:
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Tissa—the Buddha’s cousin on his father’s side—informed several mendicants:

segs.p: “api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo; disāpi me na pakkhāyanti; dhammāpi maṁ na paṭibhanti; thinamiddhañca me cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati; anabhirato ca brahmacariyaṁ carāmi; hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā”ti.
segs.e: “Reverends, my body feels like it’s drugged. I’m disorientated, the teachings don’t spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill my mind. I lead the spiritual life dissatisfied, and have doubts about the teachings.”

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.

segs.p: “āyasmā, bhante, tisso bhagavato pitucchāputto sambahulānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ evamāroceti:

‘api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo; disāpi me na pakkhāyanti; dhammāpi maṁ na paṭibhanti; thinamiddhañca me cittaṁ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati; anabhirato ca brahmacariyaṁ carāmi; hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā’”ti.
Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: So the Buddha addressed one of the monks,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena tissaṁ bhikkhuṁ āmantehī”ti.
segs.e: “Please, monk, in my name tell the mendicant Tissa that the Teacher summons him.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā tisso tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ tissaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” that monk replied. He went to Tissa and said to him,
“Reverend Tissa, the Teacher summons you.”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā tisso tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ tissaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” Tissa replied. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, tissa, sambahulānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ evamārocesi:
segs.e: “Is it really true, Tissa, that you informed several mendicants that

segs.p: ‘api me, āvuso, madhurakajāto viya kāyo …pe… hoti ca me dhammesu vicikicchā’”ti?
segs.e: your body feels like it’s drugged … and you have doubts about the teachings?”
“Yes, sir.”
“What do you think, Tissa?

segs.p: rūpe avigatarāgassa avigatacchandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa, tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti?
segs.e: If you’re not rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Good, good, Tissa!
That’s how it is, Tissa,
when you’re not rid of greed for form.
If you’re not rid of greed for feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: Yathā taṁ saṅkhāresu anigatarāgassa, viññāṇe avigatarāgassa avigatacchandassa avigatapemassa avigatapipāsassa avigatapariḷāhassa avigatataṇhassa, tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti?
segs.e: consciousness, when that consciousness decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Good, good, Tissa!
That’s how it is, Tissa,
when you’re not rid of greed for consciousness.
What do you think, Tissa?

segs.p: rūpe vigatarāgassa vigatacchandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa, tassa rūpassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti?
segs.e: If you are rid of greed, desire, fondness, thirst, passion, and craving for form, when that form decays and perishes, will it give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress?”
“No, sir.”
“Good, good, Tissa!
That’s how it is, Tissa,
when you are rid of greed for form …
feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇe vigatarāgassa vigatacchandassa vigatapemassa vigatapipāsassa vigatapariḷāhassa vigatataṇhassa tassa viññāṇassa vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti?

segs.e: consciousness.
What do you think, Tissa?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’
Suppose, Tissa, there were two individuals.

segs.p: eko puriso amaggakusalo, eko puriso maggakusalo.
segs.e: One was not skilled in the path, the other was.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ so amaggakusalo puriso amuṁ maggakusalaṁ purisaṁ maggaṁ puccheyya.
segs.e: The one not skilled in the path would question the one skilled in the path,
who would reply:
‘Come, my man, this is the path.
Go down it an hour,

segs.p: Tena muhuttaṁ gantvā dakkhissasi dvedhāpathaṁ, tattha vāmaṁ muñcitvā dakkhiṇaṁ gaṇhāhi.
segs.e: and you’ll see a fork in the road. Ignore the left, and take the right-hand path.
Go an hour more,

segs.p: Tena muhuttaṁ gantvā dakkhissasi tibbaṁ vanasaṇḍaṁ.
segs.e: and you’ll see a dense forest grove.
Go an hour more,

segs.p: Tena muhuttaṁ gantvā dakkhissasi mahantaṁ ninnaṁ pallalaṁ.
segs.e: and you’ll see an expanse of low-lying marshes.
Go an hour more,

segs.p: Tena muhuttaṁ gantvā dakkhissasi sobbhaṁ papātaṁ.
segs.e: and you’ll see a large, steep cliff.
Go an hour more,

segs.p: Tena muhuttaṁ gantvā dakkhissasi samaṁ bhūmibhāgaṁ ramaṇīyan’ti.
segs.e: and you’ll see level, cleared parkland.’

segs.p: Upamā kho myāyaṁ, tissa, katā atthassa viññāpanāya.
segs.e: I’ve made up this simile to make a point.
And this is what it means.
‘A person who is not skilled in the path’ is a term for an ordinary unlearned person.

segs.p: ‘Puriso maggakusalo’ti kho, tissa, tathāgatassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ arahato sammāsambuddhassa.
segs.e: ‘A person who is skilled in the path’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.
‘A fork in the road’ is a term for doubt.

segs.p: ‘Vāmo maggo’ti kho, tissa, aṭṭhaṅgikassetaṁ micchāmaggassa adhivacanaṁ, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: ‘The left-hand path’ is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is,
wrong view … wrong immersion.

segs.p: ‘Dakkhiṇo maggo’ti kho, tissa, ariyassetaṁ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṁ, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: ‘The right-hand path’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is,
right view … right immersion.
‘A dense forest grove’ is a term for ignorance.

segs.p: ‘Mahantaṁ ninnaṁ pallalan’ti kho, tissa, kāmānametaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘An expanse of low-lying marshes’ is a term for sensual pleasures.
‘A large, steep cliff’ is a term for anger and distress.

segs.p: ‘Samo bhūmibhāgo ramaṇīyo’ti kho, tissa, nibbānassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Level, cleared parkland’ is a term for extinguishment.
Rejoice, Tissa, rejoice!
I am here with advice, with support, with instruction.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Attamano āyasmā tisso bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinandīti.
segs.e: Satisfied, Venerable Tissa approved what the Buddha said.
Linked Discourses 22.85
9. Senior Mendicants
With Yamaka

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā sāriputto sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena yamakassa nāma bhikkhuno evarūpaṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ uppannaṁ hoti:
segs.e: Now at that time a mendicant named Yamaka had the following harmful misconception:

segs.p: “tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā”ti.
segs.e: “As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death.”

segs.p: Assosuṁ kho sambahulā bhikkhū yamakassa kira nāma bhikkhuno evarūpaṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ uppannaṁ hoti:
segs.e: Several mendicants heard this rumour.

segs.p: “tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā”ti.
Atha kho te bhikkhū yenāyasmā yamako tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā yamakena saddhiṁ sammodiṁsu.
segs.e: They went to Yamaka and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū āyasmantaṁ yamakaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him,

segs.p: “Saccaṁ kira te, āvuso yamaka, evarūpaṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ uppannaṁ:
segs.e: “Is it really true, Reverend Yamaka, that you have such a harmful misconception:

segs.p: ‘tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’”ti?
segs.e: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

segs.p: “Evaṁ khvāhaṁ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi:
segs.e: “Yes, reverends, that’s how I understand the Buddha’s teaching.”

segs.p: ‘khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’”ti.
“Mā, āvuso yamaka, evaṁ avaca, mā bhagavantaṁ abbhācikkhi. Na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhācikkhanaṁ. Na hi bhagavā evaṁ vadeyya:
segs.e: “Don’t say that, Yamaka! Don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for misrepresentation of the Buddha is not good. And the Buddha would not say that.”

segs.p: ‘khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’”ti.
Evampi kho āyasmā yamako tehi bhikkhūhi vuccamāno tatheva taṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ thāmasā parāmāsā abhinivissa voharati:
segs.e: But even though admonished by those mendicants, Yamaka obstinately stuck to that misconception and insisted on stating it.

segs.p: “tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā”ti.

Yato kho te bhikkhū nāsakkhiṁsu āyasmantaṁ yamakaṁ etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecetuṁ, atha kho te bhikkhū uṭṭhāyāsanā yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When those mendicants were unable to dissuade Yamaka from that misconception, they rose from their seats and went to see Venerable Sāriputta. They told him what had happened, and said,

segs.p: “yamakassa nāma, āvuso sāriputta, bhikkhuno evarūpaṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ uppannaṁ:
‘tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’ti.
Sādhāyasmā sāriputto yena yamako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: “May Venerable Sāriputta please go to the mendicant Yamaka out of sympathy.”
Sāriputta consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā yamako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā yamakena saddhiṁ sammodi …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṁ yamakaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of retreat, went to Venerable Yamaka and exchanged greetings with him. Seated to one side he said to Yamaka:

segs.p: “Saccaṁ kira te, āvuso yamaka, evarūpaṁ pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ uppannaṁ:
segs.e: “Is it really true, Reverend Yamaka, that you have such a harmful misconception:

segs.p: ‘tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’”ti?
segs.e: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

segs.p: “Evaṁ khvāhaṁ, āvuso, bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā”ti.
segs.e: “Yes, reverend, that’s how I understand the Buddha’s teaching.”
“What do you think, Yamaka?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, reverend.”
“Is feeling …” …
“… perception …” …
“… choices …” …
“… consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, reverend.”
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’
What do you think, Reverend Yamaka?
Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to form?”
“No, reverend.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to feeling?” …
“… perception?” …
“… choices?” …
“ … consciousness?”
“No, reverend.”
“What do you think, Reverend Yamaka?
Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to form?”
“No, reverend.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies apart from form?”
“No, reverend.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to feeling?” …
“… apart from feeling?” …
“… in relation to perception?” …
“… apart from perception?” …
“… in relation to choices?” …
“… apart from choices?” …
“… in relation to consciousness?” …
“… apart from consciousness?”
“No, reverend.”
“What do you think, Yamaka?

segs.p: rūpaṁ … vedanaṁ … saññaṁ … saṅkhāre … viññāṇaṁ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti?
segs.e: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to one who has form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”
“No, reverend.”
“What do you think, Yamaka?

segs.p: ayaṁ so arūpī … avedano … asaññī … asaṅkhāro … aviññāṇo tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti?
segs.e: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to that one who is without form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”
“No, reverend.”

segs.p: “Ettha ca te, āvuso yamaka, diṭṭheva dhamme saccato thetato tathāgate anupalabbhiyamāne, kallaṁ nu te taṁ veyyākaraṇaṁ:
segs.e: “In that case, Reverend Yamaka, since a realized one is not found by you as a genuine fact in this very life, is it cogent for you to declare:

segs.p: ‘tathāhaṁ bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāmi, yathā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṁ maraṇā’”ti?
segs.e: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, a mendicant who has ended the defilements is annihilated and destroyed when their body breaks up, and doesn’t exist after death’?”

segs.p: “Ahu kho me taṁ, āvuso sāriputta, pubbe aviddasuno pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ;
segs.e: “Reverend Sāriputta, in my ignorance, I used to have that misconception.

segs.p: idañca panāyasmato sāriputtassa dhammadesanaṁ sutvā tañceva pāpakaṁ diṭṭhigataṁ pahīnaṁ, dhammo ca me abhisamito”ti.
segs.e: But now that I’ve heard the teaching from Venerable Sāriputta, I’ve given up that misconception, and I’ve comprehended the teaching.”
“Reverend Yamaka, suppose they were to ask you:

segs.p: ‘yo so, āvuso yamaka, bhikkhu arahaṁ khīṇāsavo so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā kiṁ hotī’ti?
segs.e: ‘When their body breaks up, after death, what happens to a perfected one, who has ended the defilements?’

segs.p: Evaṁ puṭṭho tvaṁ, āvuso yamaka, kinti byākareyyāsī”ti?
segs.e: How would you answer?”
“Reverend, if they were to ask this,

segs.p: ‘yo so, āvuso yamaka, bhikkhu arahaṁ khīṇāsavo so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā kiṁ hotī’ti?

segs.e: I’d answer like this:
‘Reverend, form is impermanent.
What’s impermanent is suffering.
What’s suffering has ceased and disappeared.
Feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness is impermanent.
What’s impermanent is suffering.
What’s suffering has ceased and disappeared.’
That’s how I’d answer such a question.”
“Good, good, Reverend Yamaka!

segs.p: Tena hāvuso yamaka, upamaṁ te karissāmi etasseva atthassa bhiyyoso mattāya ñāṇāya.
segs.e: Well then, I shall give you a simile to make the meaning even clearer.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso yamaka, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo;
segs.e: Suppose there was a householder or householder’s son who was rich, with a lot of money and great wealth,
and a bodyguard for protection.

segs.p: Tassa kocideva puriso uppajjeyya anatthakāmo ahitakāmo ayogakkhemakāmo jīvitā voropetukāmo.
segs.e: Then along comes a person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten him, and take his life.
They’d think:

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ kho gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo;
segs.e: ‘This householder or householder’s son is rich, with a lot of money and great wealth,
and a bodyguard for protection.
It won’t be easy to take his life by force.
Why don’t I get close to him, then take his life?’

segs.p: So taṁ gahapatiṁ vā gahapatiputtaṁ vā upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ vadeyya:
segs.e: So he goes up to that householder or householder’s son and says:
‘Sir, I would serve you.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā upaṭṭhāpeyya.
segs.e: They would serve that householder or householder’s son.

segs.p: So upaṭṭhaheyya pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṅkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī.
segs.e: They’d get up before him and go to bed after him, and be obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.

segs.p: Tassa so gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā mittatopi naṁ saddaheyya;
segs.e: The householder or householder’s son would consider them as a friend
and companion,
and come to trust them.

segs.p: Yadā kho, āvuso, tassa purisassa evamassa:
segs.e: But when that person realizes that
