segs.p: ‘saṁvissattho kho myāyaṁ gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā’ti, atha naṁ rahogataṁ viditvā tiṇhena satthena jīvitā voropeyya.
segs.e: they’ve gained the trust of the householder or householder’s son, then, when they know he’s alone, they’d take his life with a sharp knife.
What do you think, Yamaka?

segs.p: yadā hi so puriso amuṁ gahapatiṁ vā gahapatiputtaṁ vā upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ āha:
segs.e: When that person went to the householder or householder’s son and offered to
serve him, weren’t they a killer then,
though he didn’t know that
this was his killer?

segs.p: Yadāpi so upaṭṭhahati pubbuṭṭhāyī pacchānipātī kiṅkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī, tadāpi so vadhakova.
segs.e: And when they got up before him and went to bed after him, being obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely, weren’t they a killer then,
though he didn’t know that
this was his killer?

segs.p: Yadāpi naṁ rahogataṁ viditvā tiṇhena satthena jīvitā voropeti, tadāpi so vadhakova.
segs.e: And when, knowing he was alone, they took his life with a sharp knife, weren’t they a killer then,
though he didn’t know that
this was his killer?”
“Yes, reverend.”

segs.p: “Evameva kho, āvuso, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṁ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṁ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto
segs.e: “In the same way, an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

segs.p: rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā rūpaṁ, rūpasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
They regard feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā viññāṇaṁ, viññāṇasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: They regard consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

segs.p: So aniccaṁ rūpaṁ ‘aniccaṁ rūpan’ti yathābhūtaṁ nappajānāti.
segs.e: They don’t truly understand form—which is impermanent—as impermanent.
They don’t truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is impermanent—as impermanent.
They don’t truly understand form—which is suffering—as suffering.
They don’t truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is suffering—as suffering.
They don’t truly understand form—which is not-self—as not-self.
They don’t truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is not-self—as not-self.
They don’t truly understand form—which is conditioned—as conditioned.
They don’t truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is conditioned—as conditioned.
They don’t truly understand form—which is a killer—as a killer.
They don’t truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is a killer—as a killer.

segs.p: So rūpaṁ upeti upādiyati adhiṭṭhāti ‘attā me’ti.
segs.e: They’re attracted to form, grasp it, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.
They’re attracted to feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness, grasp it, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

segs.p: Tassime pañcupādānakkhandhā upetā upādinnā dīgharattaṁ ahitāya dukkhāya saṁvattanti.
segs.e: And when you’ve gotten involved with and grasped these five grasping aggregates, they lead to your lasting harm and suffering.

segs.p: Sutavā ca kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako ariyānaṁ dassāvī …pe… sappurisadhamme suvinīto
segs.e: A learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons.

segs.p: na rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, na rūpavantaṁ attānaṁ; na attani rūpaṁ, na rūpasmiṁ attānaṁ.
segs.e: They don’t regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
They don’t regard feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: na viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, na viññāṇavantaṁ attānaṁ;
segs.e: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness,

segs.p: na attani viññāṇaṁ, na viññāṇasmiṁ attānaṁ.
segs.e: consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.

segs.p: So aniccaṁ rūpaṁ ‘aniccaṁ rūpan’ti yathābhūtaṁ pajānāti.
segs.e: They truly understand form—which is impermanent—as impermanent.
They truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is impermanent—as impermanent.
They truly understand form—which is suffering—as suffering.
They truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is suffering—as suffering.
They truly understand form—which is not-self—as not-self.
They truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is not-self—as not-self.
They truly understand form—which is conditioned—as conditioned.
They truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is conditioned—as conditioned.
They truly understand form—which is a killer—as a killer.
They truly understand feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness—which is a killer—as a killer.

segs.p: So rūpaṁ na upeti, na upādiyati, nādhiṭṭhāti: ‘attā me’ti.
segs.e: When it comes to form, they are not attracted, do not grasp, and do not fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.
When it comes to feeling …
When it comes to perception …
When it comes to choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ na upeti, na upādiyati, nādhiṭṭhāti: ‘attā me’ti.
segs.e: When it comes to consciousness, they are not attracted, do not grasp, and do not fixate on the thought, ‘my self’.

segs.p: Tassime pañcupādānakkhandhā anupetā anupādinnā dīgharattaṁ hitāya sukhāya saṁvattantī”ti.
segs.e: And when you’re not attracted to and don’t grasp these five grasping aggregates, they lead to your lasting welfare and happiness.”

segs.p: “Evametaṁ, āvuso sāriputta, hoti yesaṁ āyasmantānaṁ tādisā sabrahmacārino anukampakā atthakāmā ovādakā anusāsakā.
segs.e: “Reverend Sāriputta, this is how it is when you have such venerables as spiritual companions to advise and instruct you out of kindness and sympathy.

segs.p: Idañca pana me āyasmato sāriputtassa dhammadesanaṁ sutvā anupādāya āsavehi cittaṁ vimuttan”ti.
segs.e: And after hearing this teaching by Venerable Sāriputta, my mind is freed from the defilements by not grasping.”
Linked Discourses 22.86
9. Senior Mendicants
With Anurādha

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā anurādho bhagavato avidūre araññakuṭikāyaṁ viharati.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Buddha in a wilderness hut.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā aññatitthiyā paribbājakā yenāyasmā anurādho tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā anurādhena saddhiṁ sammodiṁsu.
segs.e: Then several wanderers of other religions went up to Venerable Anurādha and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā āyasmantaṁ anurādhaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to him:

segs.p: “yo so, āvuso anurādha, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto, taṁ tathāgato imesu catūsu ṭhānesu paññāpayamāno paññāpeti:
segs.e: “Reverend Anurādha, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them in these four ways:

segs.p: ‘hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā”ti?
segs.e: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, āyasmā anurādho te aññatitthiye paribbājake etadavoca:
segs.e: When they said this, Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers:

segs.p: “yo so āvuso tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṁ tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti:
segs.e: “Reverends, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them other than these four ways:

segs.p: ‘hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vā”ti.
segs.e: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā āyasmantaṁ anurādhaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When he said this, the wanderers said to him:

segs.p: “so cāyaṁ bhikkhu navo bhavissati acirapabbajito, thero vā pana bālo abyatto”ti.
segs.e: “This mendicant must be junior, recently gone forth, or else a foolish, incompetent senior mendicant.”

segs.p: Atha kho aññatitthiyā paribbājakā āyasmantaṁ anurādhaṁ navavādena ca bālavādena ca apasādetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṁsu.
segs.e: Then, after rebuking Venerable Anurādha by calling him “junior” and “foolish”, the wanderers rose from their seats and left.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmato anurādhassa acirapakkantesu tesu aññatitthiyesu paribbājakesu etadahosi:
segs.e: Soon after they had left, Anurādha thought:

segs.p: “sace kho maṁ te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā uttariṁ pañhaṁ puccheyyuṁ.
segs.e: “If those wanderers were to inquire further,

segs.p: Kathaṁ byākaramāno nu khvāhaṁ tesaṁ aññatitthiyānaṁ paribbājakānaṁ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assaṁ, na ca bhagavantaṁ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyaṁ, dhammassa cānudhammaṁ byākareyyaṁ, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṁ ṭhānaṁ āgaccheyyā”ti?
segs.e: how should I answer them so as to repeat what the Buddha has said, and not misrepresent him with an untruth? How should I explain in line with his teaching, so that there would be no legitimate grounds for rebuttal and criticism?”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā anurādho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā anurādho bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Anurādha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and told him all that had happened.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhante, sambahulā aññatitthiyā paribbājakā yenāhaṁ tenupasaṅkamiṁsu …pe… maṁ etadavocuṁ:
‘yo so, āvuso anurādha, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṁ tathāgato imesu catūsu ṭhānesu paññāpayamāno paññāpeti—
hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇāti vā, na hoti …
hoti ca na ca hoti, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇāti vā’”ti?
Evaṁ vuttāhaṁ, bhante, te aññatitthiye paribbājake etadavocaṁ:
“yo so, āvuso, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto, taṁ tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti:
‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇā’ti vāti.
Evaṁ vutte, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā maṁ etadavocuṁ:
‘so cāyaṁ bhikkhu na vo bhavissati acirapabbajito thero vā pana bālo abyatto’ti.
Atha kho maṁ, bhante, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā navavādena ca bālavādena ca apasādetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṁsu.
Tassa mayhaṁ, bhante, acirapakkantesu tesu aññatitthiyesu paribbājakesu etadahosi:
‘sace kho maṁ te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā uttariṁ pañhaṁ puccheyyuṁ.

Kathaṁ byākaramāno nu khvāhaṁ tesaṁ aññatitthiyānaṁ paribbājakānaṁ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assaṁ, na ca bhagavantaṁ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyaṁ, dhammassa cānudhammaṁ byākareyyaṁ, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṁ ṭhānaṁ āgaccheyyā’”ti?

segs.e: “What do you think, Anurādha?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”
“Is feeling …” …
“… perception …” …
“… choices …” …
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.” …
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’
What do you think, Anurādha?
Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to form?”
“No, sir.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to feeling?” …
“… perception?” …
“… choices?” …
“… consciousness?”
“No, sir.”
“What do you think, Anurādha?
Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to form?”
“No, sir.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies apart from form?”
“No, sir.”
“Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies in relation to feeling?” …
“… apart from feeling?” …
“… in relation to perception?” …
“… apart from perception?” …
“… in relation to choices?” …
“… apart from choices?” …
“… in relation to consciousness?” …
“… apart from consciousness?”
“No, sir.”
“What do you think, Anurādha?

segs.p: rūpaṁ … vedanā … saññā … saṅkhārā … viññāṇaṁ tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti?
segs.e: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to one who has form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”
“No, sir.”
“What do you think, Anurādha?

segs.p: ayaṁ so arūpī … avedano … asaññī … asaṅkhāro … aviññāṇo tathāgatoti samanupassasī”ti?
segs.e: Do you consider that the label ‘realized one’ applies to that one who is without form?” … “… feeling?” … “… perception?” … “… choices?” … “… consciousness?”
“No, sir.”

segs.p: “Ettha ca te, anurādha, diṭṭheva dhamme saccato thetato tathāgate anupalabbhiyamāne kallaṁ nu te taṁ veyyākaraṇaṁ:
segs.e: “In that case, Anurādha, since a realized one is not found by you as a genuine fact in this very life, is it cogent for you to declare:

segs.p: ‘yo so, āvuso, tathāgato uttamapuriso paramapuriso paramapattipatto taṁ tathāgato aññatra imehi catūhi ṭhānehi paññāpayamāno paññāpeti—
segs.e: ‘Reverends, when a Realized One is describing a realized one—a supreme person, highest of people, who has reached the highest point—they describe them other than these four ways:

segs.p: hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇāti vā … na hoti … hoti ca na ca hoti … neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṁ maraṇāti vā’”ti?
segs.e: After death, a realized one still exists, or no longer exists, or both still exists and no longer exists, or neither still exists nor no longer exists’?”
“No, sir.”
“Good, good, Anurādha!

segs.p: Pubbe cāhaṁ, anurādha, etarahi ca dukkhañceva paññapemi, dukkhassa ca nirodhan”ti.
segs.e: In the past, as today, what I describe is suffering and the cessation of suffering.”
Linked Discourses 22.87
9. Senior Mendicants
With Vakkali

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā vakkali kumbhakāranivesane viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Vakkali was staying in a potter’s shed, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā vakkali upaṭṭhāke āmantesi:
segs.e: Then he addressed his carers,

segs.p: “etha tumhe, āvuso, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha:
segs.e: “Please, reverends, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:

segs.p: ‘vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, so bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is sick, suffering, gravely ill. He bows with his head to your feet.’
And then say:

segs.p: ‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṁ upādāyā’”ti.
segs.e: ‘Sir, please go to the mendicant Vakkali out of sympathy.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied. They did as he asked.

segs.p: “vakkali, bhante, bhikkhu ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno, so bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati;
‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṁ upādāyā’”ti.

segs.e: The Buddha consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yenāyasmā vakkali tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then the Buddha robed up and, taking his bowl and robes, went to Venerable Vakkali.

segs.p: Addasā kho āyasmā vakkali bhagavantaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ. Disvāna mañcake samadhosi.
segs.e: Venerable Vakkali saw the Buddha coming off in the distance and stirred in his cot.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: But the Buddha said to him,
“It’s all right, Vakkali, don’t get up.
There are some seats spread out, I will sit there.”

segs.p: Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: He sat down on the seat spread out and said to Vakkali,

segs.p: “kacci te, vakkali, khamanīyaṁ, kacci yāpanīyaṁ, kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti, no abhikkamanti; paṭikkamosānaṁ paññāyati, no abhikkamo”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you’re keeping well, Vakkali; I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

segs.p: “Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṁ, na yāpanīyaṁ; bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti; abhikkamosānaṁ paññāyati, no paṭikkamo”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

segs.p: “Kacci te, vakkali, na kiñci kukkuccaṁ, na koci vippaṭisāro”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you don’t have any remorse or regret?”

segs.p: “Taggha me, bhante, anappakaṁ kukkuccaṁ, anappako vippaṭisāro”ti.
segs.e: “Indeed, sir, I have no little remorse and regret.”

segs.p: “Kacci pana taṁ, vakkali, attā sīlato na upavadatī”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you have no reason to blame yourself when it comes to ethical conduct?”

segs.p: “Na kho maṁ, bhante, attā sīlato upavadatī”ti.
segs.e: “No sir, I have no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct.”

segs.p: “No ce kira taṁ, vakkali, attā sīlato upavadati; atha kiñca te kukkuccaṁ ko ca vippaṭisāro”ti?
segs.e: “In that case, Vakkali, why do you have remorse and regret?”

segs.p: “Cirapaṭikāhaṁ, bhante, bhagavantaṁ dassanāya upasaṅkamitukāmo, natthi ca me kāyasmiṁ tāvatikā balamattā, yāvatāhaṁ bhagavantaṁ dassanāya upasaṅkameyyan”ti.
segs.e: “For a long time I’ve wanted to go and see the Buddha, but I was physically too weak.”

segs.p: “Alaṁ, vakkali, kiṁ te iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena?
segs.e: “Enough, Vakkali! Why would you want to see this rotting body?

segs.p: Yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṁ passati so maṁ passati;
segs.e: One who sees the teaching sees me.

segs.p: yo maṁ passati so dhammaṁ passati.
segs.e: One who sees me sees the teaching.
Seeing the teaching, you see me.
Seeing me, you see the teaching.
What do you think, Vakkali?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā”ti?
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“Suffering, sir.”

segs.p: “Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, kallaṁ nu taṁ samanupassituṁ:
segs.e: “But if it’s impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
“No, sir.”
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.” …
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ iminā ovādena ovaditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā yena gijjhakūṭo pabbato tena pakkāmi.
segs.e: And then, after giving Venerable Vakkali this advice, the Buddha rose from his seat and went to the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā vakkali acirapakkantassa bhagavato upaṭṭhāke āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Venerable Vakkali addressed his carers,

segs.p: “etha maṁ, āvuso, mañcakaṁ āropetvā yena isigilipassaṁ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkamatha.
segs.e: “Come on, reverends, lift my cot and take me to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili.

segs.p: Kathañhi nāma mādiso antaraghare kālaṁ kattabbaṁ maññeyyā”ti?
segs.e: For how on earth could one such as I imagine dying in an inhabited area!”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ mañcakaṁ āropetvā yena isigilipassaṁ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu.
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants, and did as he asked.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tañca rattiṁ tañca divāvasesaṁ gijjhakūṭe pabbate vihāsi.
segs.e: Meanwhile, the Buddha spent the rest of that night and day on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

segs.p: Atha kho dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṁ gijjhakūṭaṁ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu …pe… ekamantaṁ aṭṭhaṁsu.
segs.e: Then, late at night, two glorious deities, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ ṭhitā kho ekā devatā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: One deity said to him,
“Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is intent on liberation!”
And another deity said to him,
“He’ll definitely be well freed!”
This is what those deities said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṁsu.
segs.e: Then they bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, before vanishing right there.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassā rattiyā accayena bhikkhū āmantesi:
segs.e: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “etha tumhe, bhikkhave, yena vakkali bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā vakkaliṁ bhikkhuṁ evaṁ vadetha:
segs.e: “Come, mendicants, go to the mendicant Vakkali and tell him:

segs.p: ‘Suṇāvuso tvaṁ, vakkali, bhagavato vacanaṁ dvinnañca devatānaṁ.
segs.e: ‘Vakkali, hear the word of the Buddha and two deities.

segs.p: Imaṁ, āvuso, rattiṁ dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṁ gijjhakūṭaṁ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhaṁsu.
segs.e: Late last night, two glorious deities, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ ṭhitā kho, āvuso, ekā devatā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca—
segs.e: One deity said to him,
“Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is intent on liberation!”
The other deity said to him,

segs.p: so hi nūna, bhante, suvimutto vimuccissatīti.
segs.e: “He’ll definitely be well freed!”

segs.p: Bhagavā ca taṁ, āvuso vakkali, evamāha—
segs.e: And the Buddha said,
“Do not fear, Vakkali,
do not fear!

segs.p: Apāpakaṁ te maraṇaṁ bhavissati, apāpikā kālakiriyā’”ti.
segs.e: Your death will not be a bad one; your passing will not be a bad one.”’”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā vakkali tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” those monks replied. They went to Vakkali and said to him:
“Vakkali, hear the word of the Buddha and two deities.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā vakkali upaṭṭhāke āmantesi:
segs.e: Then Vakkali addressed his carers,
“Please, reverends, help me off my cot.

segs.p: Kathañhi nāma mādiso ucce āsane nisīditvā tassa bhagavato sāsanaṁ sotabbaṁ maññeyyā”ti.
segs.e: For how on earth could one such as I presume to listen to the Buddha’s instructions sitting on a high seat?”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ mañcakā oropesuṁ.
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” replied those mendicants, and helped him off his cot.

segs.p: “Imaṁ, āvuso, rattiṁ dve devatāyo abhikkantāya rattiyā …pe… ekamantaṁ aṭṭhaṁsu.
segs.e: They repeated what the Buddha had said.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ ṭhitā kho, āvuso, ekā devatā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
Bhagavā ca taṁ, āvuso vakkali, evamāha:
Apāpakaṁ te maraṇaṁ bhavissati, apāpikā kālakiriyā’”ti.
“Tena hāvuso, mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha:
segs.e: Vakkali said, “Well then, reverends, in my name bow with your head to the Buddha’s feet. Say to him:
‘Sir, the mendicant Vakkali is sick, suffering, gravely ill.
He bows with his head to your feet.’
And then say:
‘Form is impermanent.
I have no doubt of that.
I’m certain that what is impermanent is suffering.

segs.p: Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmi.
segs.e: And I’m certain that I have no desire or greed or fondness for what is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.
Feeling is impermanent …

segs.p: Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmi.

segs.e: Perception is impermanent …
Choices are impermanent …

segs.p: Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmi.

segs.e: Consciousness is impermanent.
I have no doubt of that.
I’m certain that what is impermanent is suffering.

segs.p: Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmī’”ti.
segs.e: And I’m certain that I have no desire or greed or fondness for what is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato vakkalissa paṭissutvā pakkamiṁsu.
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied, and left.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā vakkali acirapakkantesu tesu bhikkhūsu satthaṁ āharesi.
segs.e: And then, not long after those mendicants had left, Venerable Vakkali committed suicide.

segs.p: Atha kho te bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then those mendicants went up to the Buddha and told him Vakkali’s message.

segs.p: Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmi.
Yadaniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ, natthi me tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṁ vāti na vicikicchāmī’”ti.

segs.e: Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,
“Come, mendicants, let’s go to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili,
where Vakkali, the gentleman, committed suicide.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṁ.
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” they replied.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ yena isigilipassaṁ kāḷasilā tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then the Buddha together with several mendicants went to the Black Rock on the slopes of Isigili.

segs.p: Addasā kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ vakkaliṁ dūratova mañcake vivattakkhandhaṁ semānaṁ.
segs.e: The Buddha saw Vakkali off in the distance on his cot, lying with aggregates cast off.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena dhūmāyitattaṁ timirāyitattaṁ gacchateva purimaṁ disaṁ, gacchati pacchimaṁ disaṁ, gacchati uttaraṁ disaṁ, gacchati dakkhiṇaṁ disaṁ, gacchati uddhaṁ disaṁ, gacchati adho disaṁ, gacchati anudisaṁ.
segs.e: Now at that time a cloud of black smoke was moving east, west, north, south, above, below, and in-between.
The Buddha said to the mendicants,

segs.p: “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, etaṁ dhūmāyitattaṁ timirāyitattaṁ gacchateva purimaṁ disaṁ …pe… gacchati anudisan”ti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, do you see that cloud of black smoke moving east, west, north, south, above, below, and in-between?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Eso kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā vakkalissa kulaputtassa viññāṇaṁ samanvesati:
segs.e: “That’s Māra the Wicked searching for Vakkali’s consciousness, wondering:
‘Where is Vakkali’s consciousness established?’

segs.p: Appatiṭṭhitena ca, bhikkhave, viññāṇena vakkali kulaputto parinibbuto”ti.
segs.e: But since his consciousness is not established, Vakkali is quenched.”
Linked Discourses 22.88
9. Senior Mendicants
With Assaji

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā assaji kassapakārāme viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Assaji was staying in a monastery built by a Kassapa, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā assaji upaṭṭhāke āmantesi:
segs.e: Then he addressed his carers:

segs.p: “etha tumhe, āvuso, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamatha; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha:
segs.e: “Please, reverends, go to the Buddha, and in my name bow with your head to his feet. Say to him:
‘Sir, the mendicant Assaji is sick, suffering, gravely ill.
He bows with his head to your feet.’
And then say:

segs.p: ‘sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena assaji bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṁ upādāyā’”ti.
segs.e: ‘Sir, please go to the mendicant Assaji out of sympathy.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato assajissa paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: “Yes, reverend,” those monks replied. They did as he asked.

segs.p: sādhu kira, bhante, bhagavā yena assaji bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.

segs.e: The Buddha consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā assaji tenupasaṅkami.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to Venerable Assaji.

segs.p: Addasā kho āyasmā assaji bhagavantaṁ dūratova āgacchantaṁ.
segs.e: Venerable Assaji saw the Buddha coming off in the distance,
and stirred in his cot.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ assajiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: But the Buddha said to him,
“It’s all right, Assaji, don’t get up.
There are some seats spread out, I will sit there.”

segs.p: Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ assajiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: He sat down on the seat spread out and said,

segs.p: “kacci te, assaji, khamanīyaṁ, kacci yāpanīyaṁ …pe… paṭikkamosānaṁ paññāyati no abhikkamo”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you’re keeping well, Assaji; I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

segs.p: “Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṁ …pe… abhikkamosānaṁ paññāyati no paṭikkamo”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

segs.p: “Kacci te, assaji, na kiñci kukkuccaṁ na koci vippaṭisāro”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you don’t have any remorse or regret?”

segs.p: “Taggha me, bhante, anappakaṁ kukkuccaṁ anappako vippaṭisāro”ti.
segs.e: “Indeed, sir, I have no little remorse and regret.”

segs.p: “Kacci pana taṁ, assaji, attā sīlato na upavadatī”ti?
segs.e: “I hope you have no reason to blame yourself when it comes to ethical conduct?”

segs.p: “Na kho maṁ, bhante, attā sīlato upavadatī”ti.
segs.e: “No sir, I have no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct.”

segs.p: “No ce kira taṁ, assaji, attā sīlato upavadati, atha kiñca te kukkuccaṁ ko ca vippaṭisāro”ti?
segs.e: “In that case, Assaji, why do you have remorse and regret?”

segs.p: “Pubbe khvāhaṁ, bhante, gelaññe passambhetvā passambhetvā kāyasaṅkhāre viharāmi, sohaṁ samādhiṁ nappaṭilabhāmi.
segs.e: “Sir, before my time of illness I meditated having completely stilled the physical process. But now I can’t get immersion.

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhante, taṁ samādhiṁ appaṭilabhato evaṁ hoti:
segs.e: Since I can’t get immersion, I think:
‘May I not decline!’”

segs.p: “Ye te, assaji, samaṇabrāhmaṇā samādhisārakā samādhisāmaññā tesaṁ taṁ samādhiṁ appaṭilabhataṁ evaṁ hoti:
segs.e: “There are, Assaji, ascetics and brahmins for whom samādhi is the essence, equating immersion with the ascetic life. They think:
‘May we not decline!’
What do you think, Assaji?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.” …
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?” …
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anajjhositā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

segs.p: Dukkhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anajjhositā’ti pajānāti. ‘Anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

segs.p: Adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, sā ‘aniccā’ti pajānāti …pe… ‘anabhinanditā’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t relish it.

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaṁyutto naṁ vedayati;
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: dukkhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaṁyutto naṁ vedayati;
segs.e: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaṁyutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: So kāyapariyantikañce vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikañce vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

segs.p: ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṁ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life is over, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, assaji, telañca paṭicca, vaṭṭiñca paṭicca, telappadīpo jhāyeyya;
segs.e: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn.

segs.p: tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya.
segs.e: As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

segs.p: Evameva kho, assaji, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

segs.p: ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṁ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life is over, everything that’s felt, being no longer relished, will become cool right here.’”
Linked Discourses 22.89
9. Senior Mendicants
With Khemaka

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ sambahulā therā bhikkhū kosambiyaṁ viharanti ghositārāme.
segs.e: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā khemako badarikārāme viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
segs.e: Now at that time Venerable Khemaka was staying in the Jujube Tree Monastery, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

segs.p: Atha kho therā bhikkhū sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitā āyasmantaṁ dāsakaṁ āmantesuṁ:
segs.e: In the late afternoon those senior mendicants came out of retreat and addressed Venerable Dāsaka,

segs.p: “ehi tvaṁ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṁ bhikkhuṁ evaṁ vadehi:
segs.e: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:
‘Reverend Khemaka, the seniors

segs.p: kacci te, āvuso, khamanīyaṁ, kacci yāpanīyaṁ, kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti no abhikkamanti, paṭikkamosānaṁ paññāyati no abhikkamo’”ti?
segs.e: hope you’re keeping well; they hope you’re all right. They hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ khemakaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He went to Khemaka and said to him:
“Reverend Khemaka, the seniors
hope you’re keeping well; they hope you’re all right. They hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

segs.p: “Na me, āvuso, khamanīyaṁ na yāpanīyaṁ …pe… abhikkamosānaṁ paññāyati no paṭikkamo”ti.
segs.e: “Reverend, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said,

segs.p: ‘na me, āvuso, khamanīyaṁ …pe… abhikkamosānaṁ paññāyati no paṭikkamo’”ti.
“Ehi tvaṁ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṁ bhikkhuṁ evaṁ vadehi:
segs.e: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:
‘Reverend Khemaka, the seniors say that

segs.p: pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: these five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:
the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Imesu āyasmā khemako pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassatī’”ti?
segs.e: Do you regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self?’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā …pe…
segs.e: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

segs.p: Imesu āyasmā khemako pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassatī”ti?

segs.e: “These five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:
the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Imesu khvāhaṁ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassāmī”ti.
segs.e: I do not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said:

segs.p: Imesu khvāhaṁ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassāmī’”ti.
“Ehi tvaṁ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṁ bhikkhuṁ evaṁ vadehi:
segs.e: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:
‘Reverend Khemaka, the seniors say that

segs.p: pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: these five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:
the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: No ce kirāyasmā khemako imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassati.
segs.e: If, as it seems, Venerable Khemaka does not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self,
then he is a perfected one, with defilements ended.’”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako …pe…
segs.e: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

segs.p: no ce kirāyasmā khemako imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassati, tenahāyasmā khemako arahaṁ khīṇāsavo”ti.

segs.e: “These five grasping aggregates have been taught by the Buddha, that is:
the grasping aggregates of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Imesu khvāhaṁ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassāmi, na camhi arahaṁ khīṇāsavo;
segs.e: I do not regard anything among these five grasping aggregates as self or as belonging to self, yet I am not a perfected one, with defilements ended.

segs.p: api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṁ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmī”ti.
segs.e: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā dāsako yena therā bhikkhū …pe…
segs.e: Then Dāsaka went to those senior mendicants and told them what had happened. They said:

segs.p: pañcime, āvuso, upādānakkhandhā vuttā bhagavatā, seyyathidaṁ—
Imesu khvāhaṁ, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu na kiñci attaṁ vā attaniyaṁ vā samanupassāmi, na camhi arahaṁ khīṇāsavo;
api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṁ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmī”ti.
“Ehi tvaṁ, āvuso dāsaka, yena khemako bhikkhu tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā khemakaṁ bhikkhuṁ evaṁ vadehi:
segs.e: “Please, Reverend Dāsaka, go to the mendicant Khemaka and say to him:
‘Reverend Khemaka, the seniors ask,

segs.p: yametaṁ, āvuso khemaka, asmīti vadesi, kimetaṁ asmīti vadesi?
segs.e: when you say “I am”, what is it that you’re talking about?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ asmīti vadesi, aññatra rūpā asmīti vadesi,
segs.e: Is it form or apart from form?
Is it feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ asmīti vadesi, aññatra viññāṇā asmīti vadesi.
segs.e: consciousness, or apart from consciousness?

segs.p: Yametaṁ, āvuso khemaka, asmīti vadesi. Kimetaṁ asmīti vadesī’”ti?
segs.e: When you say “I am”, what is it that you’re talking about?”

segs.p: “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā dāsako therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ paṭissutvā yenāyasmā khemako tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ khemakaṁ etadavoca—
segs.e: “Yes, reverends,” replied Dāsaka. He relayed the message to Khemaka, who replied:

segs.p: Yametaṁ, āvuso khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadesī”ti?

segs.e: “Enough, Reverend Dāsaka! What’s the point in running back and forth?
Bring my staff,
I’ll go to see the senior mendicants myself.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā khemako daṇḍamolubbha yena therā bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā therehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then Venerable Khemaka, leaning on a staff, went to those senior mendicants and exchanged greetings with them.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ khemakaṁ therā bhikkhū etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. They said to him:
“Reverend Khemaka, when you say ‘I am’, what is it that you’re talking about?
Is it form or apart from form?
Is it feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness, or apart from consciousness?

segs.p: Yametaṁ, āvuso khemaka, ‘asmī’ti vadesi, kimetaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadesī”ti?
segs.e: When you say ‘I am’, what is it that you’re talking about?”

segs.p: “Na khvāhaṁ, āvuso, rūpaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi; napi aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: “Reverends, I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to form, or apart from form.
I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: na viññāṇaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi; napi aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: consciousness, or apart from consciousness.

segs.p: Api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṁ ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmi.
segs.e: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso, uppalassa vā padumassa vā puṇḍarīkassa vā gandho.
segs.e: It’s like the scent of a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus.

segs.p: Yo nu kho evaṁ vadeyya: ‘pattassa gandho’ti vā ‘vaṇṇassa gandho’ti vā ‘kiñjakkhassa gandho’ti vā sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti?
segs.e: Would it be right to say that the scent belongs to the petals or the stalk or the pistil?”
“No, reverend.”
“Then, reverends, how should it be said?”

segs.p: “‘Pupphassa gandho’ti kho, āvuso, sammā byākaramāno byākareyyā”ti.
segs.e: “It would be right to say that the scent belongs to the flower.”

segs.p: “Evameva khvāhaṁ, āvuso, na rūpaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi, napi aññatra rūpā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: “In the same way, reverends, I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to form, or apart from form.
I don’t say ‘I am’ with reference to feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: na viññāṇaṁ ‘asmī’ti vadāmi, napi aññatra viññāṇā ‘asmī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: consciousness, or apart from consciousness.

segs.p: Api ca me, āvuso, pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ‘asmī’ti adhigataṁ ‘ayamahamasmī’ti na ca samanupassāmi.
segs.e: For when it comes to the five grasping aggregates I’m not rid of the conceit ‘I am’. But I don’t regard anything as ‘I am this’.

segs.p: Kiñcāpi, āvuso, ariyasāvakassa pañcorambhāgiyāni saṁyojanāni pahīnāni bhavanti, atha khvassa hoti: ‘yo ca pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato asmīti māno, asmīti chando, asmīti anusayo asamūhato.
segs.e: Although a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a lingering residue of the conceit ‘I am’, the desire ‘I am’, and the underlying tendency ‘I am’ which has not been eradicated.

segs.p: So aparena samayena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati—
segs.e: After some time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

segs.p: iti rūpaṁ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo;
segs.e: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.
Such is feeling …
Such is perception …
Such are choices …

segs.p: iti viññāṇaṁ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti.
segs.e: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

segs.p: Tassimesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato yopissa hoti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṁ gacchati.
segs.e: As they do so, that lingering residue is eradicated.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, āvuso, vatthaṁ saṅkiliṭṭhaṁ malaggahitaṁ. Tamenaṁ sāmikā rajakassa anupadajjuṁ.
segs.e: Suppose there was a cloth that was dirty and soiled, so the owners give it to a launderer.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ rajako ūse vā khāre vā gomaye vā sammadditvā acche udake vikkhāleti.
segs.e: The launderer kneads it thoroughly with salt, lye, and cow dung, and rinses it in clear water.

segs.p: Kiñcāpi taṁ hoti vatthaṁ parisuddhaṁ pariyodātaṁ, atha khvassa hoti yeva anusahagato ūsagandho vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato.
segs.e: Although that cloth is clean and bright, it still has a lingering scent of salt, lye, or cow dung that had not been eradicated.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ rajako sāmikānaṁ deti. Tamenaṁ sāmikā gandhaparibhāvite karaṇḍake nikkhipanti.
segs.e: The launderer returns it to its owners, who store it in a fragrant casket.

segs.p: Yopissa hoti anusahagato ūsagandho vā khāragandho vā gomayagandho vā asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṁ gacchati.
segs.e: And that lingering scent would be eradicated.

segs.p: Evameva kho, āvuso, kiñcāpi ariyasāvakassa pañcorambhāgiyāni saṁyojanāni pahīnāni bhavanti, atha khvassa hoti yeva pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato.
segs.e: In the same way, although a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a lingering residue of the conceit ‘I am’, the desire ‘I am’, and the underlying tendency ‘I am’ which has not been eradicated.

segs.p: So aparena samayena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati.
segs.e: After some time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates.

segs.p: ‘Iti rūpaṁ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo;
segs.e: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form.
Such is feeling …
Such is perception …
Such are choices …

segs.p: iti viññāṇaṁ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti.
segs.e: Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’

segs.p: Tassa imesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato yopissa hoti pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu anusahagato ‘asmī’ti, māno ‘asmī’ti, chando ‘asmī’ti anusayo asamūhato, sopi samugghātaṁ gacchatī”ti.
segs.e: As they do so, that lingering residue is eradicated.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, therā bhikkhū āyasmantaṁ khemakaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When he said this, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Khemaka,

segs.p: “na kho mayaṁ āyasmantaṁ khemakaṁ vihesāpekhā pucchimha, api cāyasmā khemako pahosi tassa bhagavato sāsanaṁ vitthārena ācikkhituṁ desetuṁ paññāpetuṁ paṭṭhapetuṁ vivarituṁ vibhajituṁ uttānīkātuṁ.
segs.e: “We didn’t want to trouble Venerable Khemaka with our questions. But you’re capable of explaining, teaching, asserting, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing the Buddha’s instructions in detail.

segs.p: Tayidaṁ āyasmatā khemakena tassa bhagavato sāsanaṁ vitthārena ācikkhitaṁ desitaṁ paññāpitaṁ paṭṭhapitaṁ vivaritaṁ vibhajitaṁ uttānīkatan”ti.
segs.e: And that’s just what you’ve done.”
That is what Venerable Khemaka said.

segs.p: Attamanā therā bhikkhū āyasmato khemakassa bhāsitaṁ abhinanduṁ.
segs.e: Satisfied, the senior mendicants approved what Khemaka said.

segs.p: Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṁ bhaññamāne saṭṭhimattānaṁ therānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṁsu, āyasmato khemakassa cāti.
segs.e: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty senior mendicants and of Venerable Khemaka were freed from defilements by not grasping.
Linked Discourses 22.90
9. Senior Mendicants
With Channa

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ sambahulā therā bhikkhū bārāṇasiyaṁ viharanti isipatane migadāye.
segs.e: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā channo sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito avāpuraṇaṁ ādāya vihārena vihāraṁ upasaṅkamitvā there bhikkhū etadavoca:
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Channa came out of retreat. Taking a latchkey, he went from dwelling to dwelling, going up to the senior mendicants and saying,

segs.p: “ovadantu maṁ āyasmanto therā, anusāsantu maṁ āyasmanto therā, karontu me āyasmanto therā dhammiṁ kathaṁ, yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyan”ti.
segs.e: “May the venerable senior mendicants advise me and instruct me! May they give me a Dhamma talk so that I can see the teaching!”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, therā bhikkhū āyasmantaṁ channaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: When he said this, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Channa:
“Reverend Channa, form,
feeling,
perception,
choices,
and consciousness are impermanent.
Form,
feeling,
perception,
choices,
and consciousness are not-self.
All conditions are impermanent.
All things are not-self.”
Then Venerable Channa thought,
“I too think in this way. …

segs.p: Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti.
Atha ca pana me sabbasaṅkhārasamathe sabbūpadhipaṭinissagge taṇhākkhaye virāge nirodhe nibbāne cittaṁ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati nādhimuccati.
segs.e: And yet my mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided about the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.
Because of anxiety, grasping arises
and keeps turning back to the thought:
‘So who then is my self?’

segs.p: Na kho panevaṁ dhammaṁ passato hoti.
segs.e: But that doesn’t happen for someone who sees the teaching.

segs.p: Ko nu kho me tathā dhammaṁ deseyya yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyan”ti.
segs.e: Who can teach me the Dhamma so that I can see the teaching?”
Then Venerable Channa thought,

segs.p: “ayaṁ kho āyasmā ānando kosambiyaṁ viharati ghositārāme satthu ceva saṁvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṁ sabrahmacārīnaṁ, pahoti ca me āyasmā ānando tathā dhammaṁ desetuṁ yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyaṁ;
segs.e: “Venerable Ānanda is staying near Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery. He’s praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions. He’s quite capable of teaching me the Dhamma so that I can see the teaching.

segs.p: atthi ca me āyasmante ānande tāvatikā vissaṭṭhi.
segs.e: Since I have so much trust in Venerable Ānanda,
why don’t I go to see him?”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā channo senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena kosambī ghositārāmo yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṁ sammodi …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā channo āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Channa set his lodgings in order and, taking his bowl and robe, set out for Kosambī. He went to see Ānanda in Ghosita’s monastery, exchanged greetings with him, and told him what had happened. Then he said,

segs.p: “Ekamidāhaṁ, āvuso ānanda, samayaṁ bārāṇasiyaṁ viharāmi isipatane migadāye.
Atha khvāhaṁ, āvuso, sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito avāpuraṇaṁ ādāya vihārena vihāraṁ upasaṅkamiṁ;
‘ovadantu maṁ āyasmanto therā, anusāsantu maṁ āyasmanto therā, karontu me āyasmanto therā dhammiṁ kathaṁ yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyan’ti.
Evaṁ vutte, maṁ, āvuso, therā bhikkhū etadavocuṁ:
Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti.
Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe dhammā anattā’ti.
Atha ca pana me sabbasaṅkhārasamathe sabbūpadhipaṭinissagge taṇhākkhaye virāge nirodhe nibbāne cittaṁ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati nādhimuccati.
Na kho panevaṁ dhammaṁ passato hoti.
Ko nu kho me tathā dhammaṁ deseyya yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyanti.
‘ayaṁ kho āyasmā ānando kosambiyaṁ viharati ghositārāme satthu ceva saṁvaṇṇito sambhāvito ca viññūnaṁ sabrahmacārīnaṁ, pahoti ca me āyasmā ānando tathā dhammaṁ desetuṁ yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyaṁ.
Atthi ca me āyasmante ānande tāvatikā vissaṭṭhi.

segs.e: “May Venerable Ānanda advise me and instruct me! May he give me a Dhamma talk so that I can see the teaching!”

segs.p: karotu me, āyasmā ānando dhammiṁ kathaṁ yathāhaṁ dhammaṁ passeyyan”ti.
“Ettakenapi mayaṁ āyasmato channassa attamanā api nāma taṁ āyasmā channo āvi akāsi khīlaṁ chindi.
segs.e: “I’m already delighted with Venerable Channa. Hopefully you’ve opened yourself up and severed your hard-heartedness.
Listen well, Channa.
You are capable of understanding the teaching.”

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmato channassa tāvatakeneva uḷāraṁ pītipāmojjaṁ uppajji:
segs.e: Then right away Channa was filled with lofty rapture and joy,
“It seems I’m capable of understanding the teaching!”

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, āvuso channa, bhagavato sutaṁ, sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ kaccānagottaṁ bhikkhuṁ ovadantassa—
segs.e: “Reverend Channa, I heard and learned in the presence of the Buddha his advice to the mendicant Kaccānagotta:

segs.p: dvayanissito khvāyaṁ, kaccāna, loko yebhuyyena atthitañceva natthitañca.
segs.e: ‘Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on the duality of existence and non-existence.

segs.p: Lokasamudayaṁ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passato yā loke natthitā, sā na hoti.
segs.e: But for one who truly sees the origin of the world with right understanding, the concept of non-existence regarding the world does not occur.

segs.p: Lokanirodhaṁ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passato yā loke atthitā, sā na hoti.
segs.e: And for one who truly sees the cessation of the world with right understanding, the concept of existence regarding the world does not occur.
This world is for the most part shackled by getting involved, grasping, and insisting.

segs.p: taṁ cāyaṁ upayupādānaṁ cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusayaṁ na upeti na upādiyati nādhiṭṭhāti ‘attā me’ti.
segs.e: But if—for all that getting involved and grasping, mental fixation, and insistence and underlying tendency—they do not get attracted, grasp, and fixate on the thought, ‘my self’,

segs.p: Dukkhameva uppajjamānaṁ uppajjati, dukkhaṁ nirujjhamānaṁ nirujjhatīti na kaṅkhati na vicikicchati.
segs.e: they’ll have no doubt or uncertainty that what arises is just suffering arising, and what ceases is just suffering ceasing.
Their knowledge of this is independent of others.
This is how right view is defined.
“All exists”: this is one extreme.
“All does not exist”: this is the second extreme.

segs.p: Ete te, kaccāna, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṁ deseti—
segs.e: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle way:
“Ignorance is a requirement for choices.
Choices are a requirement for consciousness. …
That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
When ignorance fades away and ceases with no residue left behind, choices cease. …
That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”’”

segs.p: “Evametaṁ, āvuso ānanda, hoti yesaṁ āyasmantānaṁ tādisā sabrahmacārayo anukampakā atthakāmā ovādakā anusāsakā.
segs.e: “Reverend Ānanda, this is how it is when you have such venerables as spiritual companions to advise and instruct you out of kindness and sympathy.

segs.p: Idañca pana me āyasmato ānandassa dhammadesanaṁ sutvā dhammo abhisamito”ti.
segs.e: And now that I’ve heard this teaching from Venerable Ānanda, I’ve comprehended the teaching.”
Linked Discourses 22.91
9. Senior Mendicants
Rāhula
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā rāhulo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Rāhula went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how does one know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs?”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kiñci, rāhula, rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ rūpaṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
segs.e: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
One truly sees any kind of feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā …pe…
segs.e: consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’

segs.p: sabbaṁ viññāṇaṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya passati.
Evaṁ kho, rāhula, jānato evaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na hontī”ti.
segs.e: That’s how to know and see so that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs.”
Linked Discourses 22.92
9. Senior Mendicants
Rāhula (2nd)
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Seated to one side, Rāhula said to the Buddha:

segs.p: “kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṁ mānasaṁ hoti vidhāsamatikkantaṁ santaṁ suvimuttan”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how does one know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed?”

segs.p: “Yaṁ kiñci, rāhula, rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā …pe… yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ rūpaṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti.
segs.e: “Rāhula, one truly sees any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.
One truly sees any kind of feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ ajjhattaṁ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṁ vā sukhumaṁ vā hīnaṁ vā paṇītaṁ vā yaṁ dūre santike vā, sabbaṁ viññāṇaṁ ‘netaṁ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṁ yathābhūtaṁ sammappaññāya disvā anupādā vimutto hoti.
segs.e: One truly sees any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,’ one is freed by not grasping.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, rāhula, jānato evaṁ passato imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagataṁ mānasaṁ hoti vidhāsamatikkantaṁ santaṁ suvimuttan”ti.
segs.e: That’s how to know and see so that the heart is rid of I-making, mine-making, and conceit for this conscious body and externally for all signs; and going beyond discrimination, it’s peaceful and well freed.”
Linked Discourses 22.93
10. Flowers
A River
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, nadī pabbateyyā ohārinī dūraṅgamā sīghasotā. Tassā ubhosu tīresu kāsā cepi jātā assu, te naṁ ajjholambeyyuṁ; kusā cepi jātā assu, te naṁ ajjholambeyyuṁ; pabbajā cepi jātā assu, te naṁ ajjholambeyyuṁ; bīraṇā cepi jātā assu, te naṁ ajjholambeyyuṁ; rukkhā cepi jātā assu, te naṁ ajjholambeyyuṁ. Tassā puriso sotena vuyhamāno kāse cepi gaṇheyya, te palujjeyyuṁ. So tatonidānaṁ anayabyasanaṁ āpajjeyya. Kuse cepi gaṇheyya, pabbaje cepi gaṇheyya, bīraṇe cepi gaṇheyya, rukkhe cepi gaṇheyya, te palujjeyyuṁ. So tatonidānaṁ anayabyasanaṁ āpajjeyya.
segs.e: “Suppose, mendicants, there was a mountain river that flowed swiftly, going far, carrying all before it. If wild sugarcane, kusa grass, reeds, vetiver, or trees grew on either bank, they’d overhang the river. And if a person who was being swept along by the current grabbed the wild sugarcane, kusa grass, reeds, vetiver, or trees, it’d fall apart, and they’d come to ruin because of that.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṁ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṁ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto
segs.e: In the same way, an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons.

segs.p: rūpaṁ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā rūpaṁ, rūpasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: They regard form as self, self as having form, form in self, or self in form.
But their form falls apart,
and they come to ruin because of that.
They regard feeling …
perception …
choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ attato samanupassati, viññāṇavantaṁ vā attānaṁ; attani vā viññāṇaṁ, viññāṇasmiṁ vā attānaṁ.
segs.e: consciousness as self, self as having consciousness, consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
But their consciousness falls apart,
and they come to ruin because of that.
What do you think, mendicants?
Is form permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.” …
“Is feeling …
perception …
choices …
consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, sir.”
“So you should truly see …
Seeing this …
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”

segs.p: “Nāhaṁ, bhikkhave, lokena vivadāmi, lokova mayā vivadati.
segs.e: “Mendicants, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me.

segs.p: Na, bhikkhave, dhammavādī kenaci lokasmiṁ vivadati.
segs.e: When your speech is in line with the teaching you do not dispute with anyone in the world.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, natthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ, ahampi taṁ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: What the astute deem as not existing, I too say does not exist.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, atthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ, ahampi taṁ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: What the astute deem as existing, I too say exists.

segs.p: Kiñca, bhikkhave, natthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ, yamahaṁ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi?
segs.e: And what do the astute deem as not existing, which I too say does not exist?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ, bhikkhave, niccaṁ dhuvaṁ sassataṁ avipariṇāmadhammaṁ natthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.
Feeling …
Perception …
Choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ niccaṁ dhuvaṁ sassataṁ avipariṇāmadhammaṁ natthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, bhikkhave, natthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘natthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: This is what the astute deem as not existing, which I too say does not exist.

segs.p: Kiñca, bhikkhave, atthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ, yamahaṁ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi?
segs.e: And what do the astute deem as existing, which I too say exists?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ, bhikkhave, aniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ atthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Form that is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.
Feeling … Perception … Choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ aniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vipariṇāmadhammaṁ atthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Consciousness that is impermanent, suffering, and perishable.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, bhikkhave, atthisammataṁ loke paṇḍitānaṁ; ahampi taṁ ‘atthī’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: This is what the astute deem as existing, which I too say exists.

segs.p: Atthi, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo, taṁ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti;
segs.e: There is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

segs.p: abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā taṁ ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.
segs.e: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

segs.p: Kiñca, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo, taṁ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti, abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti?
segs.e: And what is that worldly phenomenon in the world?

segs.p: Rūpaṁ, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo taṁ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti.
segs.e: Form is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

segs.p: Abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.
segs.e: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena evaṁ ācikkhiyamāne desiyamāne paññapiyamāne paṭṭhapiyamāne vivariyamāne vibhajiyamāne uttānīkariyamāne na jānāti na passati tamahaṁ, bhikkhave, bālaṁ puthujjanaṁ andhaṁ acakkhukaṁ ajānantaṁ apassantaṁ kinti karomi.
segs.e: This being so, what can I do about a foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know or see?
Feeling …
Perception …
Choices …

segs.p: viññāṇaṁ, bhikkhave, loke lokadhammo taṁ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti.
segs.e: Consciousness is a worldly phenomenon in the world that the Realized One understands and comprehends.

segs.p: Abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti.
segs.e: Then he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, clarifies, analyzes, and discloses it.

segs.p: Yo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena evaṁ ācikkhiyamāne desiyamāne paññapiyamāne paṭṭhapiyamāne vivariyamāne vibhajiyamāne uttānīkariyamāne na jānāti na passati tamahaṁ, bhikkhave, bālaṁ puthujjanaṁ andhaṁ acakkhukaṁ ajānantaṁ apassantaṁ kinti karomi.
segs.e: This being so, what can I do about a foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know or see?

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uppalaṁ vā padumaṁ vā puṇḍarīkaṁ vā udake jātaṁ udake saṁvaḍḍhaṁ udakā accuggamma ṭhāti anupalittaṁ udakena;
segs.e: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus. Though it sprouted and grew in the water, it would rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to it.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, tathāgato loke jāto loke saṁvaḍḍho lokaṁ abhibhuyya viharati anupalitto lokenā”ti.
segs.e: In the same way, though I was born and grew up in the world, I live having mastered the world, unsullied by the world.”

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā ayujjhāyaṁ viharati gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Ayodhya on the bank of the Ganges River.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṁ gaṅgā nadī mahantaṁ pheṇapiṇḍaṁ āvaheyya. Tamenaṁ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, pheṇapiṇḍe sāro?
segs.e: “Mendicants, suppose this Ganges River was carrying along a big lump of foam. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a lump of foam?

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṁ kiñci rūpaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ …pe… yaṁ dūre santike vā taṁ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, rūpe sāro?
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in form?

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, saradasamaye thullaphusitake deve vassante udake udakapubbuḷaṁ uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca. Tamenaṁ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, udakapubbuḷe sāro?
segs.e: Suppose it was autumn, when the heavens rain heavily, and a bubble on the water forms and pops right away. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a water bubble?

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yā kāci vedanā atītānāgatapaccuppannā …pe… yā dūre santike vā taṁ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, vedanāya sāro?
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of feeling at all … examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in feeling?

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gimhānaṁ pacchime māse ṭhite majjhanhike kāle marīcikā phandati. Tamenaṁ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya …pe… kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, marīcikāya sāro?
segs.e: Suppose that in the last month of summer, at noon, a shimmering mirage appears. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a mirage?

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yā kāci saññā …pe….
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of perception at all … examining it carefully. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in perception?

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṁ caramāno tiṇhaṁ kuṭhāriṁ ādāya vanaṁ paviseyya. So tattha passeyya mahantaṁ kadalikkhandhaṁ ujuṁ navaṁ akukkukajātaṁ. Tamenaṁ mūle chindeyya; mūle chetvā agge chindeyya, agge chetvā pattavaṭṭiṁ vinibbhujeyya. So tassa pattavaṭṭiṁ vinibbhujanto pheggumpi nādhigaccheyya, kuto sāraṁ. Tamenaṁ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, kadalikkhandhe sāro?
segs.e: Suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. Wandering in search of heartwood, they’d take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There they’d see a big banana trunk, straight and young and grown unskewed. They’d cut it down at the base, cut off the top, and unroll the coiled sheaths. But they wouldn’t even find sapwood, much less heartwood. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in a banana trunk?

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ye keci saṅkhārā atītānāgatapaccuppannā …pe… ye dūre santike vā taṁ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, saṅkhāresu sāro?
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of choices at all … examining them rationally. And they appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in choices?

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, māyākāro vā māyākārantevāsī vā catumahāpathe māyaṁ vidaṁseyya. Tamenaṁ cakkhumā puriso passeyya nijjhāyeyya yoniso upaparikkheyya. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyeyya, tucchakaññeva khāyeyya, asārakaññeva khāyeyya. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, māyāya sāro?
segs.e: Suppose an illusionist or their apprentice was to demonstrate an illusion at the crossroads. And a person with clear eyes would see it and contemplate it, examining it rationally. And it would appear to them as completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in an illusion?

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṁ kiñci viññāṇaṁ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṁ …pe… yaṁ dūre santike vā, taṁ bhikkhu passati nijjhāyati yoniso upaparikkhati. Tassa taṁ passato nijjhāyato yoniso upaparikkhato rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, asārakaññeva khāyati. Kiñhi siyā, bhikkhave, viññāṇe sāro?
segs.e: In the same way, a mendicant sees and contemplates any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; solid or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—examining it rationally. And it appears to them completely vacuous, hollow, and insubstantial. For what essence could there be in consciousness?

segs.p: Evaṁ passaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi … saññāyapi … saṅkhāresupi … viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati.
segs.e: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

segs.p: Nibbindaṁ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati. Vimuttasmiṁ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṁ hoti …pe…
segs.e: Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they’re freed. When they’re freed, they know they’re freed.
They understand: ‘… there is nothing further for this place.’”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“Form is like a lump of foam;
feeling is like a bubble;
perception seems like a mirage;
choices like a banana plant;
and consciousness like an illusion:
so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.
However you contemplate them,
examining them rationally,
they’re vacuous and hollow
when you look at them closely.
Concerning this body,
he of vast wisdom has taught
that when three things are given up,
you’ll see this form discarded.
When vitality, warmth, and consciousness
leave this body,
it lies dumped there,
food for others, insentient.
Such is this continuity,
this illusion, this lament of fools.
It’s said to be a killer,
for no core is found here.
An energetic mendicant
should examine the aggregates like this,
with situational awareness and mindfulness
whether by day or by night.
They should give up all fetters,
and make a refuge for themselves.
They should live as though their head was on fire,
aspiring to the state that does not pass.”
